context: Consider a loop of thin wire in the shape of a circle of radius R (Fig. 4.1). A single electron of charge e (with e<0) and mass m is confined to move on this loop. A uniform magnetic field B is applied along the z axis, producing a magnetic vector potential A. Use cylindrical coordinates (r, θ, z). Let p̂ be the canonical momentum operator, ψ the wavefunction, E the energy, ℏ the reduced Planck constant, h the Planck constant, and c the speed of light. Denote the magnetic flux threading the loop by φ=π R^2 B and the flux quantum by φ0=−c h/e. The integer quantum number is n. The ground-state integer is denoted by n*, which is the integer nearest to e R^2 B/(2 c ℏ) (equivalently, to e φ/(c h)). In part b, j denotes the electric current density, I the total current in the loop, S the cross-sectional area of the wire, C the normalization constant, and êθ the azimuthal unit vector. Let [x] denote the greatest integer less than or or equal to x. A rough sketch of the energy versus magnetic field is shown in Fig. 4.2. In part c we will switch to SI units explicitly for the numerical estimate; in SI the flux quantum is φ0,SI=h/|e| and the approximation n≈e φ/h is used consistently with I=e^2 φ/(4 π^2 m R^2) in SI.

subquestions.subproblem: How does the ground state energy of the electron depend upon the value of the applied magnetic field in the approximation we have described? Derive a formula and give a rough picture of the result.
subquestions.solution:
Choose the gauge in cylindrical coordinates with a uniform magnetic field B along z so that A_r=0, A_θ=r B/2, and A_z=0. The time-independent Schrödinger equation for the electron in this gauge is
$$
\frac{1}{2 m} \left( \hat p - \frac{e}{c} A \right)^2 \psi = E \psi
$$
Introduce the gauge transformation
$$
\psi = \psi' \exp\left( \frac{i e}{c \hbar} \int^x A \cdot dx \right)
$$
which implies
$$
\left( \hat p - \frac{e}{c} A \right) \psi = \exp\left( \frac{i e}{c \hbar} \int^x A \cdot dx \right) \hat p \psi'
$$
and
$$
\left( \hat p - \frac{e}{c} A \right)^2 \psi = \exp\left( \frac{i e}{c \hbar} \int^x A \cdot dx \right) \hat p^2 \psi'
$$
Therefore
$$
\frac{1}{2 m} \hat p^2 \psi' = E \psi'
$$
Confining the motion to the ring r=R gives
$$
A_\theta = \frac{r B}{2}
$$
The wavefunction on the ring is
$$
\psi(\theta) = \psi'(\theta) \exp\left( \frac{i e}{c \hbar} \int_{r=R} A \cdot dx \right)
$$
Evaluate the line integral along the ring
$$
\int_{r=R} A \cdot dx = \int_0^{\theta} A_\theta R d\theta
$$
Next
$$
\int_0^{\theta} A_\theta R d\theta = \frac{B R^2}{2} \theta
$$
so that
$$
\psi(\theta) \propto \psi'(\theta) \exp\left( \frac{i e B R^2}{2 c \hbar} \theta \right)
$$
On the ring
$$
\hat p = - \frac{i \hbar}{R} \frac{d}{d\theta}
$$
The reduced equation is
$$
- \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m R^2} \frac{d^2 \psi'(\theta)}{d\theta^2} = E \psi'(\theta)
$$
with solution
$$
\psi'(\theta) = e^{i c_1 \theta}
$$
and corresponding energy
$$
E = \frac{\hbar^2 c_1^2}{2 m R^2}
$$
Single-valuedness requires
$$
\psi(\theta) = \psi(\theta + 2 \pi)
$$
which implies
$$
2 \pi \left( c_1 + \frac{e B R^2}{2 c \hbar} \right) = 2 \pi n
$$
Hence
$$
 c_1 = n - \frac{e B R^2}{2 c \hbar}
$$
The energy levels are
$$
E_n = \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m R^2} \left( n - \frac{e B R^2}{2 c \hbar} \right)^2
$$
Define the flux and the flux quantum
$$
\phi = \pi R^2 B
$$
$$
\phi_0 = - \frac{c h}{e}
$$
Then
$$
E_n = \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m R^2} \left( n + \frac{\phi}{\phi_0} \right)^2
$$
As a function of B or φ, E_n is a set of parabolas (see Fig. 4.2). The ground state energy is
$$
E_g = \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m R^2} \left( n^* - \frac{e B R^2}{2 c \hbar} \right)^2
$$
where n* is the integer nearest to e R^2 B/(2 c \hbar) or to e φ/(c h). Because e<0 for the electron, e φ/(c h) is negative, and the parabolas are centered at these values
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form E_g = ... and your response should use only the variables B, m, R, ℏ, e, c, and n*.

subquestions.subproblem: Imagine that we start with the wire in its ground state in the presence of a magnetic flux φ. Next the magnetic field is turned off. Calculate the current in the loop.
subquestions.solution:
If the system starts in the ground state with energy E_n, the integer n remains the same when B is turned off. The wavefunction on the ring is
$$
\psi(\theta) = C e^{i n \theta}
$$
The electric current density is
$$
 j = \frac{e \hbar}{2 m i} \left( \psi^* \nabla \psi - \psi \nabla \psi^* \right)
$$
Evaluated on the ring r=R, this gives
$$
 j = \frac{e \hbar n}{m R} |\psi|^2 \hat e_{\theta}
$$
Normalize over the ring of circumference 2 \pi R and cross-sectional area S
$$
\int \psi^* \psi dl dS = 1
$$
$$
2 \pi R |C|^2 S = 1
$$
$$
|C|^2 = \frac{1}{2 \pi R S}
$$
The total current is
$$
I = \int j \cdot dS
$$
so
$$
I = \frac{e \hbar n}{m R} |C|^2 S
$$
and
$$
I = \frac{e \hbar n}{2 \pi m R^2}
$$
Because the electron is initially in the ground state, the integer n equals one of the two nearest integers to e φ/(c h), namely
$$
 n = \left[ \frac{e \phi}{c h} \right]
$$
or
$$
 n = \left[ \frac{e \phi}{c h} \right] - 1
$$
where [A] denotes the greatest integer not greater than A. For a thin wire j is taken to be uniform across any cross section
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form I = ... and your response should use only the variables e, ℏ, n, m, and R. In the same response, specify n = ... using only the variables e, φ, c, and h (consistent with the ground-state convention stated in the problem). Do not include any other variables.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the current in amps assuming R = 2 cm and φ = 0.6 gauss cm^2.
subquestions.solution:
We now switch to SI units for the numerical estimate. In SI the flux quantum is φ_{0,SI}=h/|e|, and we use the approximation n≈e φ/h consistent with the SI expression for I. Parameters:
$$
R = 2 \times 10^{-2} \unit{m}
$$
$$
\phi = 0.6 \times 10^{-8} \unit{Wb}
$$
$$
e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \unit{C}
$$
$$
m = 0.9 \times 10^{-30} \unit{kg}
$$
Using I=e \hbar n/(2 \pi m R^2) with n \approx e \phi/h in SI gives
$$
I = \frac{e^2 \phi}{4 \pi^2 m R^2}
$$
Numerically this gives
$$
I \approx 1.1 \times 10^{-14} \unit{A}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the current I as a numerical value in amperes, to 2 significant figures.

grading_standard.formula: $$\left( \hat p - \frac{e}{c} A \right) \psi = \exp\left( \frac{i e}{c \hbar} \int^x A \cdot dx \right) \hat p \psi'$$
$$\left( \hat p - \frac{e}{c} A \right)^2 \psi = \exp\left( \frac{i e}{c \hbar} \int^x A \cdot dx \right) \hat p^2 \psi'$$
$$E_n = \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m R^2} \left( n - \frac{e B R^2}{2 c \hbar} \right)^2$$
$$E_g = \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m R^2} \left( n^* - \frac{e B R^2}{2 c \hbar} \right)^2$$

context: Assume nonrelativistic quantum mechanics. The Schrödinger equation for a possibly time-dependent Hamiltonian operator and wave function is given by $$i \hbar \frac{\partial \psi(t)}{\partial t} = \hat H(t) \psi(t)$$ Time reversal is implemented by mapping time as t to -t together with complex conjugation. Define the time-reversed wave function as psi_T(t). Consider an electron of charge -e, mass m, and magnetic moment operator related to the Pauli matrices. Let c denote the speed of light and \hbar the reduced Planck constant. The Pauli matrices are collected into the vector \sigma = (\sigma_x, \sigma_y, \sigma_z). The magnetic moment operator is defined by $$\pmb{\mu} = - \frac{e \hbar}{2 m c} \sigma$$ The z-component of the magnetic moment is denoted by \mu_z. The external magnetic field vector H has components H_y and H_z along the Cartesian unit vectors \hat y and \hat z, respectively, so $$H = H_y \hat y + H_z \hat z$$ The unit vectors \hat x, \hat y, \hat z denote the Cartesian spatial directions. In the electron rest frame, the Hamiltonian for a magnetic moment in a magnetic field is $$\hat H = - \pmb{\mu} \cdot H$$ Operator time evolution for operators with no explicit time dependence follows the Heisenberg equation $$\frac{dA}{dt} = \frac{1}{i \hbar} [A, \hat H]$$ where the commutator is defined by $$[A,B] = AB - BA$$ Useful Pauli matrix identities include $$\sigma_x \sigma_y = i \sigma_z$$ $$\sigma_y \sigma_z = i \sigma_x$$ $$\sigma_z \sigma_x = i \sigma_y$$

subquestions.subproblem: Assuming that nonrelativistic quantum mechanics is invariant under time reversal, derive the time reversed form of the Schrodinger wave function.
subquestions.solution: Start from the Schrödinger equation $$i \hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \psi(t) = \hat H(t) \psi(t)$$ Apply the transformation t to -t $$- i \hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \psi(-t) = \hat H(-t) \psi(-t)$$ Take the complex conjugate $$i \hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \psi^*(-t) = \hat H^*(-t) \psi^*(-t)$$ If the Hamiltonian satisfies $$\hat H^*(-t) = \hat H(t)$$ then the Schrödinger equation is covariant under time reversal, and the time-reversed wave function is $$\psi_T(t) = \psi^*(-t)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of $\psi_T(t) = \ldots$, and your response should be written with $\psi, t$.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the quantum mechanical Hamiltonian for a free electron with magnetic moment \pmb{\mu} in the external constant magnetic field H_z in the z-direction, in the reference frame of the electron?
subquestions.solution: The Hamiltonian in the electron rest frame is $$\hat H = - \pmb{\mu} \cdot H$$ For a field along z $$H = H_z \hat z$$ Hence $$\hat H = - \mu_z H_z$$ Using the z-component of the magnetic moment $$\mu_z = - \frac{e \hbar}{2 m c} \sigma_z$$ gives $$\hat H = \frac{e \hbar}{2 m c} \sigma_z H_z$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of $\hat H = \ldots$, and your response should be written with $e, \hbar, m, c, \sigma_z, H_z$.

subquestions.subproblem: Suppose that an extra constant magnetic field H_y is imposed in the y-direction. Determine the form of the quantum mechanical operator for the time rate of change of \pmb{\mu} in this case.
subquestions.solution: With the additional field, the magnetic field is $$H = H_y \hat y + H_z \hat z$$ The Hamiltonian becomes $$\hat H = \frac{e \hbar}{2 m c} \sigma_z H_z + \frac{e \hbar}{2 m c} \sigma_y H_y$$ The Heisenberg equation gives $$\frac{d \pmb{\mu}}{dt} = \frac{1}{i \hbar} [\pmb{\mu}, \hat H]$$ Using the Pauli identities, one finds $$\frac{d \pmb{\mu}}{dt} = \frac{2}{\hbar} \left( \frac{e \hbar}{2 m c} \right)^2 \sigma \times H$$ Equivalently, using \pmb{\mu} = - \frac{e \hbar}{2 m c} \sigma, this can be written as $$\frac{d \pmb{\mu}}{dt} = \frac{e}{m c} H \times \pmb{\mu}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of $\dfrac{d\pmb{\mu}}{dt} = \ldots$, and your response should be written with $e, m, c, H, \pmb{\mu}$.

grading_standard.formula: $$\hat H = \frac{e \hbar}{2 m c} \sigma_z H_z + \frac{e \hbar}{2 m c} \sigma_y H_y$$

context: A particle has mass m, charge q, intrinsic angular momentum vector s (s is not necessarily equal to ħ/2), and a magnetic dipole moment μ given by μ = g q s / 2 m c. The particle moves in a uniform magnetic field B with a velocity small compared with c. Choose the vector potential A = (1/2) B × r, where r is the position vector with Cartesian components x_i. Let P denote the canonical momentum operator with components P_i. Work in the Heisenberg picture with dO/dt = (1/iħ)[O,H], and use the commutator [A,B] = AB − BA. Spin operators satisfy [s_i, s_j] = i ħ ε_{i j k} s_k. The Levi-Civita symbol is ε_{i j k} and δ_{i j} is the Kronecker delta. Repeated indices are summed over i,j,k ∈ {1,2,3}. The magnitudes |P| and |s| denote Euclidean norms. The speed of light is c and ħ is the reduced Planck constant.

subquestions.subproblem: Write down the Hamiltonian for this system. (The vector potential for the uniform magnetic field may be written as A = B × r / 2.)
subquestions.solution:
$$H = \frac{1}{2 m} \left(P - \frac{q}{c} A\right)^2 - \mu \cdot B$$
$$H = \frac{1}{2 m} P^2 - \frac{q}{m c} A \cdot P + \frac{q^2}{2 m c^2} A^2 - \frac{g q}{2 m c} s \cdot B$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of H = ... , and your response should be written with H, P, A, s, B, m, q, g, c.

subquestions.subproblem: Derive the quantum mechanical (Heisenberg) equations of motion from this Hamiltonian, for the linear momentum P and for the angular momentum s. The A^2 term may be neglected in this nonrelativistic approximation. (Note that the results look exactly like the classical equations of motion.)
subquestions.solution:
Neglecting the A^2 term in H, for the momentum components P_i we have
$$\frac{d P_i}{d t} = \frac{1}{i \hbar} [P_i, H]$$
$$\frac{d P_i}{d t} = \frac{1}{i \hbar} \left[P_i, - \frac{q}{m c} A_j P_j\right]$$
$$\frac{d P_i}{d t} = \frac{i q}{\hbar m c} [P_i, A_j P_j]$$
$$[P_i, A_j] = - i \hbar \frac{\partial A_j}{\partial x_i}$$
$$[P_i, A_j P_j] = - i \hbar \frac{\partial A_j}{\partial x_i} P_j$$
$$\frac{d P_i}{d t} = \frac{q}{m c} \frac{\partial A_j}{\partial x_i} P_j$$
For the spin components s_i we have
$$\frac{d s_i}{d t} = \frac{1}{i \hbar} [s_i, H]$$
$$\frac{d s_i}{d t} = \frac{1}{i \hbar} \left[s_i, - \frac{g q}{2 m c} s_j B_j\right]$$
$$[s_i, s_j] = i \hbar \varepsilon_{i j k} s_k$$
$$\frac{d s_i}{d t} = - \frac{g q}{2 m c} \varepsilon_{i j k} B_j s_k$$
$$\frac{d s}{d t} = - \frac{g q}{2 m c} B \times s$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should provide the two Heisenberg equations of motion in component form as dP_i/dt = ... and ds_i/dt = ... , and your response should be written with P_i, s_i, A_j, B_j, m, q, g, c, ε_{ijk}, and (if used) the spatial derivatives ∂A_j/∂x_i.

subquestions.subproblem: Without solving these equations, identify the value of the constant g for which the helicity will remain constant. (Helicity is defined here as the cosine of the angle between the vectors P and s.)
subquestions.solution:
As P and s commute, we can work in common eigenstates. Define the helicity h by
$$h = \frac{P \cdot s}{|P| |s|}$$
For the chosen gauge, the vector potential components are
$$A_i = \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_{i j k} B_j r_k$$
The commutator with the orbital term is
$$\left[h, - \frac{q}{m c} A \cdot P\right] = \frac{- q}{m c |s| |P|} [s_i P_i, A_j P_j]$$
$$\left[h, - \frac{q}{m c} A \cdot P\right] = \frac{i \hbar q}{2 m c} \varepsilon_{i j k} \frac{s_i}{|s|} \frac{P_j}{|P|} B_k$$
The commutator with the spin term is
$$\left[h, - \frac{g q}{2 m c} s \cdot B\right] = \frac{- g q}{2 m c |s| |P|} [s_i P_i, s_j B_j]$$
$$\left[h, - \frac{g q}{2 m c} s \cdot B\right] = - \frac{i \hbar g q}{2 m c} \varepsilon_{i j k} \frac{s_i}{|s|} \frac{P_j}{|P|} B_k$$
Summing the two contributions gives
$$[h, H] = \left[h, - \frac{q}{m c} A \cdot P\right] + \left[h, - \frac{g q}{2 m c} s \cdot B\right]$$
If the helicity is a constant of motion, then
$$[h, H] = 0$$
which requires
$$g = 1$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express g as a numerical value.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the actual value of the constant g for any one of the following particles: e, p, n, \pi?
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Choose one particle from {e, p, n, π} and report the corresponding value of its g-factor as a numerical value in the form g_e = ... or g_p = ... or g_n = ... or g_π = ... , rounded to the specified number of significant figures.

grading_standard.formula: $$H = \frac{1}{2 m} P^2 - \frac{q}{m c} A \cdot P + \frac{q^2}{2 m c^2} A^2 - \frac{g q}{2 m c} s \cdot B$$
$$\frac{d P_i}{d t} = \frac{i q}{\hbar m c} [P_i, A_j P_j]$$
$$[P_i, A_j P_j] = - i \hbar \frac{\partial A_j}{\partial x_i} P_j$$
$$\frac{d P_i}{d t} = \frac{q}{m c} \frac{\partial A_j}{\partial x_i} P_j$$
$$\frac{d s_i}{d t} = \frac{1}{i \hbar} \left[s_i, - \frac{g q}{2 m c} s_j B_j\right]$$
$$\frac{d s_i}{d t} = - \frac{g q}{2 m c} \varepsilon_{i j k} B_j s_k$$
$$\left[h, - \frac{q}{m c} A \cdot P\right] = \frac{- q}{m c |s| |P|} [s_i P_i, A_j P_j]$$
$$\left[h, - \frac{q}{m c} A \cdot P\right] = \frac{i \hbar q}{2 m c} \varepsilon_{i j k} \frac{s_i}{|s|} \frac{P_j}{|P|} B_k$$
$$\left[h, - \frac{g q}{2 m c} s \cdot B\right] = \frac{- g q}{2 m c |s| |P|} [s_i P_i, s_j B_j]$$
$$\left[h, - \frac{g q}{2 m c} s \cdot B\right] = - \frac{i \hbar g q}{2 m c} \varepsilon_{i j k} \frac{s_i}{|s|} \frac{P_j}{|P|} B_k$$
$$[h, H] = \left[h, - \frac{q}{m c} A \cdot P\right] + \left[h, - \frac{g q}{2 m c} s \cdot B\right]$$

context:
In a neutron interferometer (see Fig. 4.3), a monochromatic neutron beam is split by Bragg reflection at point A into two coherent paths and recombined at point D. The incident neutron wavelength is
$$
\lambda=\frac{289}{200} \unit{Å}
$$
Arm 2 contains a region of uniform, static magnetic field along a path length l, while arm 1 contains no magnetic field. The magnetic field vector in arm 2 is defined by
$$
B_{vec}=B_0 n_B
$$
where B_0 is the field magnitude and n_B is a unit vector along the field direction. The neutron is uncharged and spin-\frac{1}{2} with intrinsic magnetic moment \mu with \mu<0, mass m, speed v, and de Broglie wave number k. Planck’s constant is h and the reduced constant is
$$
\hbar=\frac{h}{2\pi}
$$
The Pauli matrices are collected as the vector \sigma. The position vector is r. The total wavefunction is factorized into spatial and spin parts as
$$
\Psi(r,t)=\psi_r(r,t)\chi(t)
$$
The Hamiltonian operator in the field region is H with energy eigenvalue E. The entrance and exit times of the field region on arm 2 are t_0 and t_1. Let \chi_D^{(1)} and \chi_D^{(2)} denote the spin-state amplitudes at D from arms 1 and 2, respectively. Let I_0 be a field-independent constant set by the interferometer optics, and let I_D be the detected intensity for a given input spin state. Define I_D^{(+)} as the intensity at D when the incident neutron spin is initially polarized parallel to n_B, and I_D^{(-)} as the intensity when it is initially polarized anti-parallel to n_B. For convenience define the phase
$$
\alpha=\frac{2\pi\mu m l \lambda B_0}{h^2}
$$
and let
$$
\eta=\pm 1
$$
denote the eigenvalue of \sigma\cdot n_B corresponding to spin polarized parallel (\eta=+1) or anti-parallel (\eta=-1) to n_B. Find explicit expressions for I_D^{(+)}(B_0,l,\lambda) and I_D^{(-)}(B_0,l,\lambda).
solution:
In the uniform magnetic field region the time-independent Schrodinger equation is
$$
\left(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2-\mu\sigma\cdot B_{vec}\right)\Psi=E\Psi
$$
The time evolution from entrance at t_0 to exit at t_1 is
$$
\Psi(t_1)=\exp\left(-\frac{i}{\hbar}H\left(t_1-t_0\right)\right)\Psi(t_0)
$$
The spatial part evolves as a free particle in the uniform field region
$$
\psi_r(r,t_1)=\exp\left(-\frac{i}{\hbar}\left(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2\right)\left(t_1-t_0\right)\right)\psi_r(r,t_0)
$$
The spin part undergoes Larmor evolution
$$
\chi(t_1)=\exp\left(\frac{i}{\hbar}\mu\sigma\cdot B_{vec}\left(t_1-t_0\right)\right)\chi(t_0)
$$
The traversal time through the field region is
$$
 t_1-t_0=\frac{l}{v}
$$
The de Broglie wave number is
$$
 k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}
$$
The dispersion relation gives
$$
 k=\frac{mv}{\hbar}
$$
Combining these results yields
$$
\chi(t_1)=\exp\left(i\frac{2\pi\mu m l \lambda}{h^2}\sigma\cdot B_{vec}\right)\chi(t_0)
$$
Using the field decomposition
$$
B_{vec}=B_0 n_B
$$
we obtain
$$
\chi(t_1)=\exp\left(i\alpha\sigma\cdot n_B\right)\chi(t_0)
$$
The spin-state amplitudes at D are
$$
\chi_D^{(1)}=\chi(t_0)
$$
$$
\chi_D^{(2)}=\exp\left(i\alpha\sigma\cdot n_B\right)\chi(t_0)
$$
The detected intensity for a given input spin state is
$$
I_D=I_0\left\|\chi_D^{(1)}+\chi_D^{(2)}\right\|^2
$$
Using the identity
$$
\exp\left(i\alpha\sigma\cdot n_B\right)=\cos\alpha+i\left(\sigma\cdot n_B\right)\sin\alpha
$$
For an incident spin eigenstate of \sigma\cdot n_B with eigenvalue
$$
\eta=\pm 1
$$
we have
$$
\left|1+e^{i\eta\alpha}\right|^2=4\cos^2\frac{\alpha}{2}
$$
Absorbing the overall scale into I_0 gives
$$
I_D^{(+)}=I_0\cos^2\frac{\alpha}{2}
$$
$$
I_D^{(-)}=I_0\cos^2\frac{\alpha}{2}
$$
Substituting the definition of \alpha gives
$$
I_D^{(+)}=I_0\cos^2\frac{\pi\mu m l \lambda B_0}{h^2}
$$
$$
I_D^{(-)}=I_0\cos^2\frac{\pi\mu m l \lambda B_0}{h^2}
$$
Because of the cosine squared, the sign of \mu does not affect the final intensity
final_answer_instructions: Provide two algebraic expressions for the detected intensities as functions of B_0, l, and \lambda. Your final answer should be given in the form I_D^{(+)} = ... and I_D^{(-)} = ..., and your response should be written only with the symbols I_0, \mu, m, l, \lambda, B_0, h (and standard constants such as \pi). Do not introduce any additional variables or leave the result in terms of \alpha or other intermediate symbols.

context: Consider the one-dimensional motion of an uncharged particle of spin 1/2 and magnetic moment mu confined in an infinite square well extending from x = -L to x = L, so the spatial wave function vanishes at x = -L and x = L. The magnetic moment is defined by the spin operator s and a positive constant mu_0 via $$\mu = - \frac{2 \mu_0}{\hbar} s$$ In region I (x < 0) there is a uniform magnetic field of magnitude B_0 in the z direction, $$B = B_0 e_z$$ In region II (x > 0) there is a uniform field of the same magnitude in the x direction, $$B = B_0 e_x$$ Here e_x and e_z are unit vectors in the x and z directions. The unperturbed Hamiltonian is H_0, the perturbation is H', and the total Hamiltonian is H = H_0 + H'. The perturbation is the Zeeman coupling $$H' = - \mu \cdot B$$ Using s = (\hbar/2) sigma, where sigma is the Pauli vector, this becomes $$H' = \mu_0 \sigma \cdot B$$ Inside the well this implies H' = \mu_0 B_0 \sigma_z in region I and H' = \mu_0 B_0 \sigma_x in region II. The particle mass is m and \hbar is the reduced Planck constant. In part (b), the notation k_1 and k_2 denotes the spatial wave numbers in regions I and II, respectively, determined by the common energy E through the dispersion relations given there. The spin basis eigenvectors of sigma_z are taken as z\uparrow = (1,0)^T and z\downarrow = (0,1)^T, and those of sigma_x are proportional to x\uparrow = (1,1)^T and x\downarrow = (1,-1)^T.

subquestions.subproblem: Use perturbation theory to find the ground state energy and ground state wave function (both space and spin parts) in the weak field limit B_0 \ll (\hbar / L)^2 / 2 m \mu_0
subquestions.solution: In the absence of the magnetic field, H = H_0 and the normalized spatial eigenfunctions are $$\psi_n(x) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{L}} \sin \frac{n \pi (x + L)}{2 L}$$ The corresponding energies are $$E_n = \frac{\pi^2 \hbar^2 n^2}{8 m L^2}$$ The quantum number is $$n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$$ Each spatial level is twofold degenerate due to spin. The perturbation is $$H' = - \mu \cdot B$$ Using s = (\hbar/2) sigma and the given relation for mu, we obtain $$H' = \mu_0 \sigma \cdot B$$ In region I, $$H' = \mu_0 B_0 \sigma_z$$ In region II, $$H' = \mu_0 B_0 \sigma_x$$ For the ground spatial state n = 1, choose the degenerate basis $$u_1 = \psi_1(x) \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$$ $$u_2 = \psi_1(x) \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$$ By symmetry, $$\int_{-L}^{0} |\psi_1(x)|^2 dx = \frac{1}{2}$$ $$\int_{0}^{L} |\psi_1(x)|^2 dx = \frac{1}{2}$$ The nonzero perturbation matrix elements are $$H'_{11} = \frac{\mu_0 B_0}{2}$$ $$H'_{22} = - \frac{\mu_0 B_0}{2}$$ $$H'_{12} = \frac{\mu_0 B_0}{2}$$ $$H'_{21} = \frac{\mu_0 B_0}{2}$$ The secular equation for the first-order shifts E^{(1)} is $$\left( \frac{\mu_0 B_0}{2} - E^{(1)} \right) \left( - \frac{\mu_0 B_0}{2} - E^{(1)} \right) - \left( \frac{\mu_0 B_0}{2} \right)^2 = 0$$ The solutions are $$E^{(1)} = \pm \frac{\mu_0 B_0}{\sqrt{2}}$$ Therefore, the ground state energy is $$E_0 = E_1 - \frac{\mu_0 B_0}{\sqrt{2}}$$ where $$E_1 = \frac{\pi^2 \hbar^2}{8 m L^2}$$ Let the corresponding ground-state spinor in the basis {u_1, u_2} be proportional to $$\begin{pmatrix} 1 - \sqrt{2} \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$$ Hence the ground state wave function is $$\varphi_0(x) = \psi_1(x) \begin{pmatrix} 1 - \sqrt{2} \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of “E0 = …” and “φ0(x) = …”. For the energy, write E0 solely in terms of the symbols m, L, ħ, μ0, and B0. For the wave function, write φ0(x) as ψ1(x) multiplied by a 2-component column spinor expressed in the {z↑, z↓} basis; if you choose to write ψ1(x) explicitly, it must be the normalized n = 1 infinite-square-well eigenfunction on [−L, L] and may only involve x and L.

subquestions.subproblem: Now consider fields with B_0 of arbitrary strength. Find the general form of the energy eigenfunction \psi_{\mathrm{I}} (both space and spin parts) in region I which satisfies the left-hand boundary condition. Find also the form \psi_{\mathrm{II}} that the eigenfunction has in region II which satisfies the right-hand boundary condition ( Fig. 4.5
subquestions.solution: In region I ( -L \le x \le 0 ), the general spatial solution that satisfies the left boundary condition \psi(-L) = 0 is $$\psi_{\mathrm{I},k_1}(x) = A \sin \big( k_1 (x + L) \big)$$ In region I the spin quantization axis is z, with eigenvectors z\downarrow = (0,1)^T and z\uparrow = (1,0)^T. The corresponding eigenfunctions and energies are $$\psi_{\mathrm{I},k_1, z\downarrow}(x) = A \sin \big( k_1 (x + L) \big) \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$$ $$E = \frac{\hbar^2 k_1^2}{2 m} - \mu_0 B_0$$ $$\psi_{\mathrm{I},k_1, z\uparrow}(x) = A \sin \big( k_1 (x + L) \big) \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$$ $$E = \frac{\hbar^2 k_1^2}{2 m} + \mu_0 B_0$$ In region II (0 \le x \le L), the general spatial solution that satisfies the right boundary condition \psi(L) = 0 is $$\psi_{\mathrm{II},k_2}(x) = C \sin \big( k_2 (x - L) \big)$$ In region II the spin quantization axis is x, with eigenvectors proportional to x\downarrow = (1,-1)^T and x\uparrow = (1,1)^T. The corresponding eigenfunctions and energies are $$\psi_{\mathrm{II},k_2, x\downarrow}(x) = C \sin \big( k_2 (x - L) \big) \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$$ $$E = \frac{\hbar^2 k_2^2}{2 m} - \mu_0 B_0$$ $$\psi_{\mathrm{II},k_2, x\uparrow}(x) = C \sin \big( k_2 (x - L) \big) \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$$ $$E = \frac{\hbar^2 k_2^2}{2 m} + \mu_0 B_0$$ Here k_1 and k_2 are the wave numbers in regions I and II related to the common energy E by the relations shown above. The full eigenfunctions are obtained by matching the two-component spinor and its spatial derivative at x = 0, but only the region-wise forms that satisfy the boundary conditions at x = -L and x = L are required here
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the forms “ψI(x) = …” and “ψII(x) = …”, where ψI(−L) = 0 and ψII(L) = 0 are manifest. Each expression must be written as a product of: (i) an overall amplitude (A for region I, C for region II); (ii) a spatial factor depending on k1 (region I) or k2 (region II) that enforces the respective boundary condition; and (iii) a 2-component spinor expressed in the σz eigenbasis {z↑, z↓} for region I and in the σx eigenbasis {x↑, x↓} for region II. Use only A, C, k1, k2, x, L, and the basis labels in these two expressions. Additionally, state the dispersion relations that link the common energy E to k1 and k2 using only E, m, ħ, μ0, and B0.

context: Consider an infinitely long solenoid carrying a steady current I that produces a constant magnetic field B confined to the interior of the solenoid. In the exterior region, B=0 but a vector potential A may be nonzero with ∇×A=B. A particle of charge e and mass m moves in the exterior region and is described by the Schrödinger equation. Work in units with ℏ=1, and let c denote the speed of light. Let V(x) be a given scalar potential in the exterior region, and let p=−i∇ be the momentum operator. For I=0, assume a stationary solution of the form $$\psi_0(x,t)=e^{i E_0 t}\psi_0(x)$$ where E0 is the energy eigenvalue. In what follows, x_ref denotes an arbitrary fixed reference point in the exterior region to be used as the lower limit for line integrals of A.

subquestions.subproblem: Write down and solve the Schrödinger equation in the region outside the solenoid for the case I≠0. Use the reference point x_ref as the lower limit for any line integral of A. Keep ℏ=1.
subquestions.solution:
For I=0, the Schrödinger equation is $$i rac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi_0(x,t)=\left[ rac{1}{2m}p^2+V(x)ight]\psi_0(x,t)$$ with $$p=-i
abla$$ In the presence of a vector potential A, minimal coupling gives the Schrödinger equation $$i rac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi(x,t)=\left[ rac{1}{2m}\left(-i
abla- rac{e}{c}Aight)^2+V(x)ight]\psi(x,t)$$ with $$
abla	imes A=B$$ Define $$\psi(x,t)=\psi_1(x,t)\exp\left(i rac{e}{c}\int_{x_{\mathrm{ref}}}^{x}A\cdot dx'ight)$$ Then ψ1 satisfies $$i rac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi_1(x,t)=\left[ rac{1}{2m}p^2+V(x)ight]\psi_1(x,t)$$ Hence $$\psi_1(x,t)=\psi_0(x,t)$$ Therefore the solution for I≠0 in the exterior region is $$\psi(x,t)=e^{i E_0 t}\psi_0(x)\exp\left(i rac{e}{c}\int_{x_{\mathrm{ref}}}^{x}A\cdot dx'ight)$$

subquestions.subproblem: Consider a two-slit diffraction experiment for the particles described above (see Fig. 4.6). Let d be the slit separation and l be the distance from the slits to the screen. Let ΔS denote the lateral shift of the interference fringes on the screen. Let f be the probability amplitude at a point on the screen, with contributions f_+ and f_- from paths passing through the upper and lower slits along paths c_+ and c_-, respectively. Let φ be the magnetic flux threading the solenoid. Let k be the particle wave number for energy E0. Assume l≫d and that ΔS is small. Hint: Write $$\psi(x,t)=\psi_0(x,t)\psi_A(x)$$ where $$\left(\nabla-i\frac{e}{c}\delta A(x)\right)\psi_A(x)=0$$ and define δA(x)≡A(x)−A_0(x), with A_0 any reference vector potential that yields zero flux through the solenoid, so that ∇×δA=0 in the exterior region.
subquestions.solution: When I=0, the amplitude at a screen point is $$f=f_+ + f_-$$ When I≠0, the path-dependent phases give $$f_+'=\exp\left(i\frac{e}{c}\int_{c_+}^{x}A\cdot dx'\right)f_+$$ $$f_-'=\exp\left(i\frac{e}{c}\int_{c_-}^{x}A\cdot dx'\right)f_-$$ The total amplitude is $$f'=f_+'+f_-'$$ Removing a common overall phase does not affect the interference pattern, and the relative phase is $$\Delta\theta=\frac{e}{c}\oint A\cdot dx$$ By Stokes' theorem, $$\Delta\theta=\frac{e}{c}\int(\nabla\times A)\cdot ds$$ Hence $$\Delta\theta=\frac{e}{c}\int B\cdot ds$$ Therefore $$\Delta\theta=\frac{e\phi}{c}$$ For small angles in the two-slit geometry, the fringe shift satisfies $$\Delta S\cdot\frac{d}{l}\cdot k=\frac{e\phi}{c}$$ Hence $$\Delta S=\frac{e l \phi}{c d k}$$ With ℏ=1 and particle energy E0, the wave number is $$k=\sqrt{2 m E_0}$$ Therefore $$\Delta S=\frac{e l \phi}{c d \sqrt{2 m E_0}}$$ This treatment is valid in the nonrelativistic regime
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \Delta S = ..., and your response should be written with e, l, \phi, c, d, m, E_0.

subquestions.subproblem: What are the energies and energy eigenfunctions for a nonrelativistic particle of mass m moving on a ring of radius R threaded by a magnetic flux phi, with the standard single-valuedness condition Psi(theta+2 pi)=Psi(theta) imposed
subquestions.solution: The single-valuedness condition is $$\Psi(\theta+2\pi)=\Psi(\theta)$$ Define $$\alpha=\frac{q\phi}{2\pi\hbar}$$ Define $$\beta=\sqrt{\frac{2 I E}{\hbar^2}}$$ The quantization condition is $$\alpha\pm\beta=n$$ where $$n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,\ldots$$ Therefore the energies are $$E_n=\frac{\hbar^2}{2 I}\left(n-\frac{q\phi}{2\pi\hbar}\right)^2$$ The normalized eigenfunctions are $$\psi_n(\theta)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{i n \theta}$$ with $$n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,\ldots$$

The Hamiltonian with minimal coupling is $$\hat H= rac{1}{2 m}  ig(p-q A ig)^2$$ With $$p=-i\hbar

context: We use time-independent, non-degenerate perturbation theory. Definitions used throughout: H is the total Hamiltonian, H_0 is the unperturbed Hamiltonian, and H' is a small perturbation such that H = H_0 + H'. The unperturbed ground state is phi_0 with energy E_0, satisfying H_0 phi_0 = E_0 phi_0. The exact ground-state wavefunction is Psi, expanded in the unperturbed basis {|phi_n>}, where H_0 |phi_n> = E_n |phi_n>. The coefficients lambda_n are small expansion parameters. The first-order ground-state energy correction is Delta E_0, given by Delta E_0 = <phi_0| H' |phi_0>. Bra-ket notation denotes inner products. For the nuclear model in part b, m is the nucleon mass and hbar is the reduced Planck constant. The spherical infinite well of radius R is described by V_sp(r) = 0 for r < R and V_sp(r) = infinity for r > R. The ellipsoidal infinite well is V_el(x,y,z) = 0 inside the ellipsoid x^2/b^2 + y^2/b^2 + z^2/a^2 = 1 and V_el = infinity otherwise, with semi-axes a ≈ R (1 + 2 beta / 3), b ≈ R (1 − beta / 3), and a small deformation parameter beta << 1. A coordinate transformation x = (b/R) xi, y = (b/R) eta, z = (a/R) zeta maps the ellipsoid to the sphere xi^2 + eta^2 + zeta^2 = R^2. We use r^2 = xi^2 + eta^2 + zeta^2 and the spherically symmetric ground-state wavefunction for the spherical infinite well phi_0(r) = sqrt(2/R) sin(pi r / R) / r. The Laplacian is denoted by nabla^2. Final numerical answers should be written explicitly as variables equal to expressions, for example Delta E_0 = 0.

subquestions.solution:
Assuming H' is small, expand the exact ground state as $$\Psi = | \phi_0 angle + \sum_{n 
e 0} \lambda_n | \phi_n angle$$ The stationary Schrodinger equation is $$ ig( H_0 + H'  ig) | \Psi angle =  ig( E_0 + \Delta E_0  ig) | \Psi angle$$ Keeping only first-order terms gives $$H' | \phi_0 angle + H_0 \sum_{n 
e 0} \lambda_n | \phi_n angle = \Delta E_0 | \phi_0 angle + E_0 \sum_{n 
e 0} \lambda_n | \phi_n angle$$ Projecting onto \langle phi_0 | and using orthonormality yields $$\Delta E_0 = \langle \phi_0 | H' | \phi_0 angle$$

Calculate the approximate change in the ground state energy E_0 due to the ellipticity of the non-spherical nucleus by finding an appropriate H' and using the result obtained in part a.

context: Employing non-degenerate first-order perturbation theory, calculate the energies of the first three stationary states n=1,2,3 for a particle of mass μ in a one-dimensional infinite square well of width a with impenetrable walls at x=0 and x=a. The portion AB of the well has been sliced off so that the resulting perturbation is linear inside the well; OA is a straight line as indicated in Fig. 5.1. The perturbation Hamiltonian is H'=(V_0/a)x for 0≤x≤a, where V_0 is a constant. Let ψ_n^0 and E_n^0 denote the unperturbed eigenfunctions and eigenvalues, and let E_n denote the perturbed energies to first order. Use ℏ for the reduced Planck constant.
solution:
The perturbation is
$$
H'=\frac{V_0}{a}x
$$
$$
0\leq x\leq a
$$
The unperturbed eigenfunctions and eigenvalues are
$$
\psi_1^0=\sqrt{\frac{2}{a}}\sin\frac{\pi x}{a}
$$
$$
E_1^0=\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2\mu a^2}
$$
$$
\psi_2^0=\sqrt{\frac{2}{a}}\sin\frac{2\pi x}{a}
$$
$$
E_2^0=\frac{2\pi^2\hbar^2}{\mu a^2}
$$
$$
\psi_3^0=\sqrt{\frac{2}{a}}\sin\frac{3\pi x}{a}
$$
$$
E_3^0=\frac{9\pi^2\hbar^2}{2\mu a^2}
$$
The first-order energy corrections are
$$
\langle\psi_1^0|H'|\psi_1^0\rangle=\frac{V_0}{2}
$$
$$
\langle\psi_2^0|H'|\psi_2^0\rangle=\frac{V_0}{2}
$$
$$
\langle\psi_3^0|H'|\psi_3^0\rangle=\frac{V_0}{2}
$$
Thus, the energies of the first three states to first order are
$$
E_1=\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2\mu a^2}+\frac{V_0}{2}
$$
$$
E_2=\frac{2\pi^2\hbar^2}{\mu a^2}+\frac{V_0}{2}
$$
$$
E_3=\frac{9\pi^2\hbar^2}{2\mu a^2}+\frac{V_0}{2}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as three algebraic equations for the first-order perturbed energies: E_1 = ..., E_2 = ..., and E_3 = .... Express each right-hand side solely in terms of μ, a, ℏ, and V_0.

context:
A particle of mass m moves one-dimensionally along the x axis in the harmonic oscillator potential with angular frequency ω. The potential is

$$
V(x)=\frac{1}{2} m \omega^{2} x^{2}
$$

In the nonrelativistic limit, the kinetic energy T and momentum p are related by

$$
T=\frac{p^{2}}{2 m}
$$

and the ground-state energy is

$$
E_{0}^{(0)}=\frac{1}{2} \hbar \omega
$$

Let E denote the total relativistic energy, c the speed of light in vacuum (SI unit \unit{m/s}), and \hbar the reduced Planck constant. Allow for relativistic corrections in the relation between T and p and compute the ground-state level shift \Delta E to order

$$
\frac{1}{c^{2}}
$$

using first-order perturbation theory. Use the ground-state wavefunction

$$
\phi_{0}(x)=\left(\frac{m \omega}{\pi \hbar}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}} \exp\left(-\frac{m \omega}{2 \hbar} x^{2}\right)
$$

and the momentum operator

$$
\hat p=- i \hbar \frac{d}{dx}
$$

where i is the imaginary unit. Define the perturbation Hamiltonian as

$$
H'=-\frac{p^{4}}{8 m^{3} c^{2}}
$$
solution:
In relativistic motion, the kinetic energy T is

$$
T=E-m c^{2}
$$

and

$$
E=\sqrt{m^{2} c^{4}+p^{2} c^{2}}
$$

Therefore

$$
T=m c^{2}\left(1+\frac{p^{2}}{m^{2} c^{2}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}-m c^{2}
$$

Expanding to order \frac{1}{c^{2}}

$$
T\approx m c^{2}\left(1+\frac{p^{2}}{2 m^{2} c^{2}}-\frac{p^{4}}{8 m^{4} c^{4}}\right)-m c^{2}
$$

which gives

$$
T\approx \frac{p^{2}}{2 m}-\frac{p^{4}}{8 m^{3} c^{2}}
$$

Thus the perturbation Hamiltonian is

$$
H'=-\frac{p^{4}}{8 m^{3} c^{2}}
$$

The first-order ground-state energy shift is

$$
\Delta E=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \phi_{0}^{*} H' \phi_{0} dx
$$

Using the operator identities

$$
\hat p=- i \hbar \frac{d}{dx}
$$

$$
\hat p^{4}=\hbar^{4} \frac{d^{4}}{dx^{4}}
$$

we write

$$
\Delta E=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \phi_{0}^{*} \left(-\frac{\hat p^{4}}{8 m^{3} c^{2}}\right) \phi_{0} dx
$$

With the explicit ground-state wavefunction

$$
\phi_{0}(x)=\left(\frac{m \omega}{\pi \hbar}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}} \exp\left(-\frac{m \omega}{2 \hbar} x^{2}\right)
$$

the integral evaluates to

\Delta E=-\frac{15}{32} \frac{(\hbar \omega)^{2}}{m c^{2}}
$$

context: An electron moves in a Coulomb field centered at the origin. Neglect spin and relativistic corrections. For the principal quantum number n=2, the unperturbed level is 4-fold degenerate with the states |n,l,m_l> = |2,0,0> and |2,1,m_l> for m_l=-1,0,1. We treat to first order the non-central perturbation V_{pert} defined by V_{pert}=f(r) x y, where f(r) is a central radial function that decays sufficiently fast as r goes to infinity. Work entirely within the n=2 degenerate subspace spanned by |2,l,m_l>. Use standard spherical coordinates (r,theta,phi), where r is the radial distance, theta is the polar angle from the positive z axis, and phi is the azimuthal angle about the z axis, with Cartesian-spherical relations given below. Define the first-order shift of an energy eigenvalue by Delta E. Let N_{levels} denote the number of distinct first-order energy levels within the n=2 manifold. For any value X of a first-order shift, let g_X denote the degeneracy of the level with Delta E=X. The Cartesian-spherical relations are: $$x=r sin theta cos phi$$ $$y=r sin theta sin phi$$ $$z=r cos theta$$ In particular, $$x y=r^2 sin^2 theta sin phi cos phi$$ and therefore $$x y=\frac{r^2}{2} sin^2 theta sin 2 phi$$ The azimuthal dependence implies that nonzero angular matrix elements inside the n=2 subspace require the magnetic quantum numbers to differ by two, i.e., $$\Delta m_l=\pm 2$$ In part c, you should express all first-order shifts in terms of a positive constant A, as defined in the solution.

subquestions.subproblem: How many distinct energy levels are there?
subquestions.solution: The perturbation is $$V_{pert}=f(r) x y$$ Using the spherical-coordinate relations above, its angular part is proportional to sin^2 theta sin 2 phi, so within the n=2 subspace the only nonvanishing couplings satisfy $$\Delta m_l=\pm 2$$ There is no l=2 state in the n=2 manifold, so |2,0,0> has no partner and its diagonal matrix element vanishes by the phi integral. Similarly, |2,1,0> has no m_l=\pm 2 partner in l=1, and its diagonal element also vanishes. Only the pair |2,1,1> and |2,1,-1> couples and splits. Therefore the n=2 level splits into three distinct first-order energies, so $$N_{levels}=3$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express N_{levels}, the number of distinct first-order energy levels within the n=2 manifold, as a single integer value.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the degeneracy of each?
subquestions.solution: Define the positive constant $$A=|\langle 2,1,1|V_{pert}|2,1,-1\rangle|$$ and $$A>0$$ The coupled pair |2,1,1> and |2,1,-1> diagonalizes into two nondegenerate levels at shifts +A and -A, while |2,0,0> and |2,1,0> remain unshifted and degenerate. The degeneracies are $$g_{+A}=1$$ $$g_{-A}=1$$ $$g_0=2$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should list the degeneracies as numerical values for g_{+A}, g_{-A}, and g_{0}, where g_X denotes the degeneracy of the level with Delta E = X.

subquestions.subproblem: Given the energy shift, call it A (A > 0), for one of the levels, what are the values of the shifts for all the others?
subquestions.solution: Let the three first-order shifts be labeled by subscripts +, -, and 0. They are $$\Delta E_{+}=A$$ $$\Delta E_{-}=-A$$ $$\Delta E_{0}=0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \(\Delta E_{+} = \ldots\), \(\Delta E_{-} = \ldots\), and \(\Delta E_{0} = \ldots\), written solely in terms of A.

context: A particle of mass m moves in a one-dimensional infinite square well of width l, with potential V(x)=infinity for x<=0 and x>=l, and V(x)=0 for 0<x<l. A small uniform potential dip of depth b (b>0) is added over the left half of the well, treated as a perturbation: V^{(1)}(x)=-b for 0<x<l/2 and V^{(1)}(x)=0 for l/2<=x<l. Using first-order non-degenerate perturbation theory, find the first-order corrected energy of the ground state. Let E^{(0)} and psi^{(0)}(x) denote the unperturbed ground-state energy and wave function, E^{(1)} the first-order energy correction, and E the ground-state energy accurate to first order in b. Use hbar for the reduced Planck constant.
solution:
For the unperturbed infinite square well, the ground-state energy and wave function are
$$
E^{(0)}=\frac{\pi^{2}hbar^{2}}{2ml^{2}}
$$
$$
\psi^{(0)}(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{l}}\sin\frac{\pi x}{l}
$$
The first-order energy correction is
$$
E^{(1)}=\int_{0}^{\frac{l}{2}}\psi^{(0)}(x)(-b)\psi^{(0)}(x)dx
$$
Using the unperturbed wave function gives
$$
E^{(1)}=-\frac{2b}{l}\int_{0}^{\frac{l}{2}}\sin^{2}\frac{\pi x}{l}dx
$$
Using the trigonometric identity
$$
\sin^{2}\theta=\frac{1}{2}(1-\cos2\theta)
$$
we obtain
$$
E^{(1)}=-\frac{b}{l}\int_{0}^{\frac{l}{2}}\left(1-\cos\frac{2\pi x}{l}\right)dx
$$
Evaluating the integral yields
$$
E^{(1)}=-\frac{b}{2}
$$
The ground-state energy to first order is
$$
E=E^{(0)}+E^{(1)}
$$
$$
E=\frac{\pi^{2}hbar^{2}}{2ml^{2}}-\frac{b}{2}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given explicitly as E = [expression], using only the symbols hbar, m, l, and b (and numerical constants). Do not introduce any additional variables.

context: A nonrelativistic particle of mass mu is confined in a one-dimensional infinitely deep square well extending from x=0 to x=L. Two identical, narrow perturbing square potentials of width a and height V are added, one centered at x=L/4 and the other at x=3L/4, with a<<L/100. Let hbar be the reduced Planck constant and n=1,2,3,... the quantum number. The unperturbed stationary states have energies E_n^(0) and normalized wave functions psi_n(x). Using first-order time-independent perturbation theory, the first-order energy shift is E_n^(1)=H'_{nn}, where H'_{nn} is the diagonal matrix element of the perturbing potential in the unperturbed basis. Compute E_2^(1)-E_4^(1) to leading order in a, treating each narrow potential by the mean value approximation about its center. Define all symbols: x is position, L is the well width, a is the perturbation width, V is the perturbation height, mu is the particle mass, hbar is the reduced Planck constant, n is the positive integer quantum number, E_n^(0) and psi_n(x) are the unperturbed energy and wave function, and E_n^(1)=H'_{nn} is the first-order shift.
solution:
The unperturbed energy levels are
$$
E_n^{(0)}=\frac{\pi^2 hbar^2}{2 mu L^2} n^2
$$
The unperturbed wave functions are
$$
\psi_n(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{L}}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}
$$
The first-order energy shift equals the diagonal matrix element of the perturbation
$$
E_n^{(1)}=H_{nn}'
$$
The matrix element is the sum of contributions from the two narrow potentials
$$
H_{nn}'=\int_{L/4-a/2}^{L/4+a/2} V\cdot\frac{2}{L}\sin^2\frac{n\pi x}{L} dx+\int_{3L/4-a/2}^{3L/4+a/2} V\cdot\frac{2}{L}\sin^2\frac{n\pi x}{L} dx
$$
For a<<L/100, apply the mean value approximation about each center to obtain
$$
H_{nn}'=\frac{2Va}{L}\left(\sin^2\frac{\pi n}{4}+\sin^2\frac{3\pi n}{4}\right)
$$
Therefore, the change in the energy difference between levels n=2 and n=4 is
$$
E_2^{(1)}-E_4^{(1)}=\frac{2Va}{L}\left(\sin^2\frac{\pi}{2}+\sin^2\frac{3\pi}{2}-\sin^2\pi-\sin^2 3\pi\right)
$$
which evaluates to
$$
E_2^{(1)}-E_4^{(1)}=\frac{4Va}{L}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of E_2^{(1)} - E_4^{(1)} = ..., and your response should be written only with V, a, and L.

grading_standard.formula: $$H_{nn}'=\int_{L/4-a/2}^{L/4+a/2} V\cdot\frac{2}{L}\sin^2\frac{n\pi x}{L} dx+\int_{3L/4-a/2}^{3L/4+a/2} V\cdot\frac{2}{L}\sin^2\frac{n\pi x}{L} dx$$

context: A particle of mass m moves in one dimension along coordinate x in the potential V(x) shown in Fig. 5.4. The parameter a>0 sets the length scale, and the box has infinitely high walls at x=-3a and x=3a. The potential is specified by regions as follows: outside the box, for |x|>3a, the potential is infinite; inside the box, for a<x<3a and -3a<x<-a, the potential is zero; in the central region, for -a<x<a, the potential equals V_0. The reduced Planck constant is denoted by \hbar. Treat the system as an infinite square well of length 6a with a perturbing potential in the central region. Use first-order nondegenerate perturbation theory to find the ground-state energy to first order. Let n=1,2,\dots be the quantum number labeling the unperturbed stationary states. Let E^{(0)} be the unperturbed energy, \psi^{(0)}(x) the corresponding normalized unperturbed wavefunction, E^{(1)} the first-order energy correction, and E the ground-state energy including the first-order correction. The perturbation operator is defined by \hat V(x)=V_0 for -a\le x\le a and \hat V(x)=0 elsewhere inside the well.
solution:
$$V(x)=\infty$$
for |x|>3a

$$V(x)=0$$
for a<x<3a and -3a<x<-a

$$V(x)=V_0$$
for -a<x<a

$$E^{(0)}=\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2 n^2}{72 m a^2}$$
for n=1,2,\dots

$$\psi^{(0)}(x)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3a}}\cos\frac{n\pi x}{6a}$$
for n an odd integer

$$\psi^{(0)}(x)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3a}}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{6a}$$
for n an even integer

context:
A one-dimensional simple harmonic oscillator of mass m and angular frequency \omega is subjected to a small perturbing potential W(x)=\lambda/(x^2+a^2), producing a dimple at the center of the motion. The Hamiltonian is
$$H=\frac{P^2}{2m}+\frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x^2+\frac{\lambda}{x^2+a^2}$$
For convenience define the unperturbed potential V and the perturbation \delta V as
$$V=\frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x^2$$
$$\delta V=\frac{\lambda}{x^2+a^2}$$
Equivalently, the Hamiltonian can be written as
$$H=\frac{P^2}{2m}+V+\delta V$$
Here P is the momentum operator, x is the position, \hbar is the reduced Planck constant, and \lambda and a are positive constants characterizing the perturbation. Calculate the first-order correction \Delta E to the ground-state energy in the two regimes: (a) \(a\ll\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}\), (b) \(a\gg\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}\). In the solution, the dimensionless substitution y=x/a may be used.

subquestions.subproblem:
Hints: the normalized ground state wave function of a simple harmonic oscillator is
$$\psi_0(x)=\left(\frac{m\omega}{\pi\hbar}\right)^{1/4}\exp\left(-\frac{m\omega x^2}{2\hbar}\right)$$
and the integral
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{x^2+a^2}=\frac{\pi}{a}$$
subquestions.solution:
For the regime
$$a\gg\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}$$
Introduce the dimensionless variable
$$y=\frac{x}{a}$$
The first-order correction to the ground-state energy is
$$\Delta E=\frac{\lambda}{a}\left(\frac{m\omega}{\pi\hbar}\right)^{1/2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{m\omega a^2}{\hbar}y^2\right)}{y^2+1}dy$$
For \(a\gg\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}\), the dominant contribution comes from small y, so \(1/(y^2+1)\approx 1\), giving
$$\Delta E\approx\frac{\lambda}{a}\left(\frac{m\omega}{\pi\hbar}\right)^{1/2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\exp\left(-\frac{m\omega a^2}{\hbar}y^2\right)dy$$
Using the Gaussian integral \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-\beta y^2}dy=\sqrt{\pi/\beta}\) with \(\beta=m\omega a^2/\hbar\), the result is
$$\Delta E=\frac{\lambda}{a^2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of ΔE = ..., and your response should be written using only λ and a (no other variables or constants).

context: A perfectly elastic point-mass ball of mass m bounces frictionlessly between two parallel, rigid walls whose separation is L=L(t). The right wall moves slowly and uniformly so that the walls are brought closer together, with speed v_1 and rate dL/dt<0 satisfying v_1=-dL/dt. The ball's instantaneous momentum magnitude is p, and its kinetic energy is E=p^2/(2m). Just before colliding with the right wall while moving to the right, the ball's speed is denoted v_2'. Immediately after that collision, it moves to the left with speed v_2. Successive collisions with the right wall are separated, to leading order in v_1, by the interval Δt=2L/v_2. In the quantum analysis, the particle is a one-dimensional particle in an infinite square well of width L with stationary energies E_n=n^2 π^2 ħ^2/(2 m L^2) for integers n≥1. Symbols used: m (mass), p (momentum magnitude), E (kinetic energy), L (wall separation), v_1 (right-wall speed), v_2', v_2 (ball speeds immediately before and after a right-wall collision), Δt (time between successive right-wall collisions), Δp (momentum change in one collision), n (quantum number), E_n (energy level), ħ (reduced Planck constant). Neglect gravity and all dissipative effects.

subquestions.subproblem: Using classical mechanics, calculate the change in energy per unit time of the ball as the walls are slowly and uniformly moved closer together.
subquestions.solution:
In classical mechanics, the kinetic energy is
$$E=\frac{p^2}{2m}$$
Therefore,
$$\frac{dE}{dt}=\frac{p}{m}\frac{dp}{dt}$$
Because the collision with the moving right wall is perfectly elastic, the relative speed before and after is unchanged, so
$$v_2'+v_1=v_2+(-v_1)$$
Hence,
$$v_2'-v_2=-2v_1$$
The momentum change in one collision is
$$\Delta p=m(v_2'-v_2)$$
Therefore,
$$\Delta p=-2mv_1$$
Using a finite-difference estimate,
$$\frac{dE}{dt}\approx\frac{p}{m}\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$$
The time between successive right-wall collisions is
$$\Delta t=\frac{2L}{v_2}$$
Substituting gives
$$\frac{dE}{dt}\approx\frac{p}{m}\frac{-2mv_1}{2L/v_2}$$
Thus,
$$\frac{dE}{dt}\approx-\frac{p v_1 v_2}{L}$$
Using
$$v_2=\frac{p}{m}$$
we obtain
$$\frac{dE}{dt}=-\frac{p^2}{mL}v_1$$
With
$$E=\frac{p^2}{2m}$$
this becomes
$$\frac{dE}{dt}=-\frac{2E}{L}v_1$$
Since the walls move closer at rate dL/dt<0 with v_1=-\frac{dL}{dt}, we get
$$\frac{dE}{dt}=-\frac{2E}{L}\frac{dL}{dt}$$
which is the desired classical rate of change of the ball's energy
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be a single explicit expression for the rate of change of energy, written as dE/dt = ..., using only the variables E, L, and dL/dt.

subquestions.subproblem: Show that this change in energy is the same as the quantum mechanical result if the ball’s quantum number does not change.
subquestions.solution:
For a stationary state in an infinite well,
$$E_n=\frac{n^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}$$
Differentiating with respect to time gives
$$\frac{dE_n}{dt}=\frac{n^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{2m}(-2)L^{-3}\frac{dL}{dt}$$
Therefore,
$$\frac{dE_n}{dt}=-\frac{2E_n}{L}\frac{dL}{dt}$$
which is the same as the classical result when the quantum number n does not change
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be a single explicit expression for the rate of change of the quantum energy level, written as dE_n/dt = ..., using only the variables E_n, L, and dL/dt.

subquestions.subproblem: If the ball is in the quantum state with n = 1, under what conditions of wall motion will it remain in that state? (Chicago)
subquestions.solution:
If the energy change during one collision is much smaller than the level spacing E_2-E_1, the state n=1 is maintained. Using
$$E=\frac{p^2}{2m}$$
we have
$$\Delta E=\frac{p}{m}\Delta p$$
Using the collision result for a slowly moving wall,
$$\Delta p=-2mv_1$$
Also,
$$p=\sqrt{2mE}$$
Therefore,
$$\Delta E=-2\sqrt{2mE}\,v_1$$
The adiabatic condition is
$$E_2-E_1\gg|\Delta E|$$
With
$$E_n=\frac{n^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}$$
we get
$$E_2-E_1=\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}(2^2-1^2)$$
Thus,
$$\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}(2^2-1^2)\gg2\sqrt{2m\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}}\,|v_1|$$
which yields
$$|v_1|\ll\frac{3\pi\hbar}{4mL}$$
Hence, the right-wall speed must satisfy |v_1| much smaller than 3πħ/(4mL) for the state n=1 to be preserved
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be a single inequality that bounds the magnitude of the wall speed, written as an explicit condition on |v_1| using only the variables v_1, m, L, and ħ.

context: Consider an electron of mass m confined to a one-dimensional infinite square well extending from x=0 to x=a. The well length is a=1 \unit{\AA}. The potential is V(x)=0 inside the well and V(x)=\infty outside the well, so the stationary-state wavefunctions vanish at the walls. The reduced Planck constant is denoted by \hbar, and E denotes the energy eigenvalue that appears in the time-independent Schrödinger equation. Let \psi_n(x) denote the normalized stationary-state wavefunctions and E_n their corresponding energy eigenvalues. In part (c), at time t=0 the system is in the state with quantum number n=1. At t=0, a rectangular perturbing potential of depth V_0=-10^{4} \unit{eV}, centered at x=a/2 and of total width 2b=10^{-12} \unit{cm}, is switched on for a duration t_0=5\times 10^{-18} \unit{s} and then removed. Let H'_{n1} be the matrix element of the perturbation between states n and 1, \omega_{n1}=(E_n-E_1)/\hbar the corresponding transition angular frequency, and P_n the probability to find the system in state n after removal of the perturbation.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the first 4 wave functions (normalize the wave functions) and sketch them).
subquestions.solution: Inside the well the time-independent Schrödinger equation is $$\frac{d^2 \psi}{dx^2} + \frac{2 m E}{\hbar^2} \psi = 0$$ with boundary conditions $$\psi(0)=0$$ $$\psi(a)=0$$ The potential is $$V(x)=0$$ for 0 \le x \le a, and $$V(x)=\infty$$ otherwise. The normalized stationary-state solutions are $$\psi_n(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{a}} \sin\left(\frac{n \pi x}{a}\right)$$ valid for 0 \le x \le a, with $$n=1,2,3,\ldots$$ For this problem the well length is $$a=1 \unit{\AA}$$ The first four normalized wavefunctions correspond to n=1,2,3,4 and have nodes at x=0 and x=a as given by the formula above
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as psi_1(x)=..., psi_2(x)=..., psi_3(x)=..., and psi_4(x)=..., written only with the variables x and a. You may alternatively present a single general expression psi_n(x)=... and explicitly specify n=1,2,3,4.

subquestions.subproblem: Compute the corresponding 4 energy levels and sketch an energy level diagram.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express E_1, E_2, E_3, and E_4 as numerical values in eV, each rounded to 3 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: At $t = 0$ , the particle is known to be in the state for which $n = \mathbf { 1 }$ . At $t = 0 .$ , a rectangular potential well $V _ { 0 } = - 1 0 ^ { 4 } \mathrm { e V }$ centered at a/2 and of width $1 0 ^ { - 1 2 } \mathrm { c m } ,$ is suddenly introduced into the well and kept there for $5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 1 8 }$ set, at which time it is removed. After removal of the perturbation, what is the probability that the system will be found in each of the states $\mathbf { n } = 2$ ,, $n = 3 ,$ , and $\mathrm { n } = 4 ?$ (The height and width of the potential well is characteristic of a neutron interacting with an electron). Note: you can use your sketch to help you estimate the relevant matrix elements.
subquestions.solution: The probability to find the system in state n after the perturbation is $$P_n=\left| H'_{n1} \frac{1 - e^{i \omega_{n1} t_0}}{\hbar \omega_{n1}} \right|^2$$ Equivalently, $$P_n=\left[ \frac{2 H'_{n1}}{\hbar \omega_{n1}} \sin\left( \frac{\omega_{n1} t_0}{2} \right) \right]^2$$ with $$\omega_{n1}=\frac{E_n - E_1}{\hbar}$$ and $$H'_{n1}=\int_{a/2 - b}^{a/2 + b} \psi_n^{*}(x) V_0 \psi_1(x) dx$$ For a very narrow well b \ll a, using the mean value theorem at x \approx a/2, $$H'_{n1} \approx \frac{4 b V_0}{a} \sin\left(\frac{n \pi}{2}\right)$$ Thus $$H'_{21}=0$$ $$H'_{41}=0$$ Using a=1 \unit{\AA}=10^{-8} \unit{cm} and 2b=10^{-12} \unit{cm}, we find for n=3 $$H'_{31}=2 \unit{eV}$$ Therefore $$P_2=0$$ $$P_4=0$$ and $$P_3=\frac{16}{\hbar^{2} \omega_{31}^{2}} \sin^{2}\left( \frac{\omega_{31} t_0}{2} \right)$$ Using the energy difference $$\hbar \omega_{31}=E_3 - E_1$$ with $$E_3=336.6 \unit{eV}$$ $$E_1=37.4 \unit{eV}$$ $$\hbar \omega_{31}=299.2 \unit{eV}$$ and the duration $$t_0=5 \times 10^{-18} \unit{s}$$ we obtain $$P_3=1.45 \times 10^{-4}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express P_2, P_3, and P_4 as numerical values, each rounded to 3 significant figures.

context: A particle of charge q and mass m is bound in a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator potential V(x) = (1/2) k x^2. A uniform static electric field of magnitude E is applied along the x-direction. Using time-independent nondegenerate perturbation theory, calculate the shift of the ground-state energy up to order E^2. Let H0 be the unperturbed harmonic-oscillator Hamiltonian, H' = - q E x the perturbation, and En^(0) = (n + 1/2) \hbar \omega the unperturbed energies for n = 0, 1, 2, ... . Define \omega = \sqrt{k/m}, \alpha = \sqrt{m \omega/\hbar}, and let \hbar be the reduced Planck constant. The ground state of H0 is denoted by |0\rangle, and \langle x|0\rangle is its position-space wave function. The Kronecker delta \delta_{ab} equals 1 if a = b and 0 otherwise. In sums with a prime, the term with n = 0 is excluded. Denote by \Delta E_0^{(2)} the second-order correction to the ground-state energy.
solution:
Choose the x-axis along the electric field
$$
H = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{d^2}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{2} k x^2 - q E x
$$
The unperturbed Hamiltonian is
$$
H_0 = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{d^2}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{2} k x^2
$$
The perturbation is
$$
H' = - q E x
$$
The ground-state wave function is identified as
$$
\psi_0(x) = \langle x|0\rangle
$$
Its explicit form is
$$
\psi_0(x) = \left(\frac{\alpha}{\pi}\right)^{1/4} \exp\big(-\frac{1}{2} \alpha^2 x^2\big)
$$
The oscillator parameters are
$$
\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}
$$
$$
\alpha = \sqrt{\frac{m \omega}{\hbar}}
$$
Because \psi_0(x) is even and x is odd, the first-order correction vanishes
$$
E_0^{(1)} = \langle 0|H'|0\rangle
$$
$$
E_0^{(1)} = 0
$$
The position matrix elements are
$$
\langle n'|x|n\rangle = \frac{1}{\alpha} \left[ \sqrt{\frac{n'}{2}} \, \delta_{n,n'-1} + \sqrt{\frac{n'+1}{2}} \, \delta_{n,n'+1} \right]
$$
Hence
$$
H'_{0n} = - q E \langle 0|x|n\rangle
$$
$$
H'_{0n} = - \frac{q E}{\sqrt{2} \alpha} \delta_{n,1}
$$
The unperturbed energies are
$$
E_n^{(0)} = \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right) \hbar \omega
$$
The second-order shift is
$$
\Delta E_0^{(2)} = \sum_{n}' \frac{|H'_{0n}|^2}{E_0^{(0)} - E_n^{(0)}}
$$
Only n = 1 contributes, giving
$$
\Delta E_0^{(2)} = - \frac{q^2 E^2}{2 \hbar \omega \alpha^2}
$$
Using
$$
\alpha^2 = \frac{m \omega}{\hbar}
$$
we obtain
$$
\Delta E_0^{(2)} = - \frac{q^2 E^2}{2 m \omega^2}
$$
In the primed sum, the term with n = 0 is excluded
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \Delta E_0^{(2)} = ... , and your response should be written using only the variables q, E, m, and \omega (and numerical constants). Do not introduce any additional variables.

context: For a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator of mass M and angular frequency \omega_0, define the dimensionless coordinate y and the scaled energy \varepsilon_n by $$y=x \sqrt{\frac{M \omega_0}{\hbar}}$$ $$\varepsilon_n=\frac{2 E_n}{\hbar \omega_0}$$ In these variables, the time-independent Schrödinger equation has kinetic energy operator T and potential energy V given by $$T=-\frac{1}{2} \frac{d^2}{dy^2}$$ $$V=\frac{1}{2} y^2$$ The stationary eigenstates |n\rangle satisfy $$\varepsilon_n=2 n+1$$ $$E_n=\hbar \omega_0 \left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)$$ Use |n\rangle to denote the nth energy eigenstate, and \delta_{i,j} for the Kronecker delta. subquestions.subproblem: Using the fact that the only non-vanishing dipole matrix element is $$\langle n+1| y | n \rangle=\sqrt{\frac{n+1}{2}}$$ and its Hermitian conjugate, find values for all the non-vanishing matrix elements of y^3 that connect to the ground state |0\rangle.
subquestions.solution: As $$\langle p| y | n \rangle=\sqrt{\frac{p}{2}} \delta_{n,p-1}+\sqrt{\frac{n}{2}} \delta_{p,n-1}$$ the non-vanishing matrix elements connected to |0\rangle are $$\langle p| y^3 | 0 \rangle=\sum_{r,s} \langle p| y | r \rangle \langle r| y | s \rangle \langle s| y | 0 \rangle$$ These occur for p=3 with r=2, s=1 and for p=1 with r=0, s=1 or r=2, s=1, namely $$\langle 3| y^3 | 0 \rangle=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$ $$\langle 1| y^3 | 0 \rangle=\frac{3}{2 \sqrt{2}}$$

subquestions.subproblem: The oscillator is perturbed by a cubic potential $$V_1=\alpha y^3$$ Find the correction to the ground state energy in the lowest non-vanishing order.
subquestions.solution: Because \psi_0 is an even function, $$\langle 0| y^3 | 0 \rangle=0$$ so the first-order energy correction vanishes. The second-order correction in the scaled units is $$\Delta E_2=\sum_{n \ne 0} \frac{|\langle 0| \alpha y^3 | n \rangle|^2}{1-\varepsilon_n}$$ Since only n=1 and n=3 contribute, $$\Delta E_2=|\alpha|^2 \left( \frac{|\langle 0| y^3 | 1 \rangle|^2}{1-\varepsilon_1}+\frac{|\langle 0| y^3 | 3 \rangle|^2}{1-\varepsilon_3} \right)$$ Using $$\varepsilon_n=\frac{2 E_n}{\hbar \omega_0}$$ $$\varepsilon_n=2 n+1$$ we have $$\Delta E_2=|\alpha|^2 \left( \frac{|\langle 0| y^3 | 1 \rangle|^2}{-2}+\frac{|\langle 0| y^3 | 3 \rangle|^2}{-6} \right)$$ With $$\langle 0| y^3 | 1 \rangle=\frac{3}{2 \sqrt{2}}$$ $$\langle 0| y^3 | 3 \rangle=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$ the result is $$\Delta E_2=-\frac{11}{16} |\alpha|^2$$
