context: Consider a hydrogenlike ionized atom (Z, A) with only a single bound electron. A uniform external magnetic field of magnitude B is applied along the z axis. Use e for the magnitude of the elementary charge, m_e for the electron mass, c for the speed of light, and ℏ for the reduced Planck constant. Let the canonical momentum operator be denoted by p̂. Let l̂ and ŝ be the electron orbital and spin angular momentum operators, respectively, and ĵ = l̂ + ŝ the total angular momentum operator with quantum numbers j and projection m_j. The z components are l̂_z, ŝ_z, and ĵ_z. The Coulomb potential is V(r) = −Z e^2/r, and ξ(r) denotes the standard radial function appearing in the spin–orbit interaction term ξ(r) ŝ · l̂ of the hydrogenlike fine-structure Hamiltonian. Define the Pauli operator σ̂_z by σ̂_z = 2 ŝ_z/ℏ. Define the Larmor frequency by ω_L = e B/(2 m_e c). For the electron case, the unperturbed fine-structure energies (in zero magnetic field) are E_{n l j} for eigenstates |n l j m_j⟩. For the spin-0 case in part (b), let m be the magnetic quantum number of l̂_z and let E_{n l} denote the corresponding unperturbed energy in zero magnetic field, independent of m. The symbol s̄_z denotes the expectation value ⟨j m_j| ŝ_z |j m_j⟩. The principal quantum number is n. Calculate the Zeeman splitting in the n = 2 state in a weak magnetic field.

subquestions.subproblem: for an electron
subquestions.solution:
Choose the z axis along the external magnetic field B. In the weak-field regime for an electron, spin–orbit coupling cannot be neglected, leading to the anomalous Zeeman effect. The full Hamiltonian is
$$
\hat H = \frac{\hat p^2}{2 m_e} - \frac{Z e^2}{r} + \frac{e B}{2 m_e c} \big( \hat l_z + 2 \hat s_z \big) + \xi(r) \hat s \cdot \hat l
$$
It is convenient to rewrite this as
$$
\hat H = H_0 + \frac{e B}{2 m_e c} \hat j_z + \frac{e B}{2 m_e c} \hat s_z
$$
with
$$
H_0 = \frac{\hat p^2}{2 m_e} - \frac{Z e^2}{r} + \xi(r) \hat s \cdot \hat l
$$
and
$$
\hat j_z = \hat l_z + \hat s_z
$$
The unperturbed eigenvalue equation is
$$
H_0 \psi_{n l j m_j} = E_{n l j} \psi_{n l j m_j}
$$
with allowed total angular momenta
$$
j = l \pm \frac{1}{2}
$$
The expectation value of ĵ_z gives
$$
\langle j m_j | \hat j_z | j m_j \rangle = m_j \hbar
$$
so the energy including the ĵ_z term is
$$
E_{n l j} + m_j \hbar \omega_L
$$
with
$$
\omega_L = \frac{e B}{2 m_e c}
$$
The additional weak-field contribution of the ŝ_z term is
$$
\omega_L \bar s_z = \frac{\hbar \omega_L}{2} \langle j m_j | \hat \sigma_z | j m_j \rangle
$$
For j = l + \frac{1}{2} this gives
$$
\frac{m_j}{2 j} \hbar \omega_L
$$
For j = l - \frac{1}{2} this gives
$$
- \frac{m_j}{2 j + 2} \hbar \omega_L
$$
Hence the total energy in the weak field is
$$
E_{n l j m_j} = E_{n l j} + \Big(1 + \frac{1}{2 j}\Big) m_j \hbar \omega_L
$$
for j = l + \frac{1}{2}, and
$$
E_{n l j m_j} = E_{n l j} + \Big(1 - \frac{1}{2 j + 2}\Big) m_j \hbar \omega_L
$$
for j = l - \frac{1}{2}. Specializing to n = 2, for the 2s_{1/2} level we have
$$
E_{2,0,\frac{1}{2}, m_j} = E_{2,0,\frac{1}{2}} + 2 m_j \hbar \omega_L
$$
with
$$
m_j = \pm \frac{1}{2}
$$
For the 2p_{3/2} level we have
$$
E_{2,1,\frac{3}{2}, m_j} = E_{2,1,\frac{3}{2}} + \frac{4}{3} m_j \hbar \omega_L
$$
with
$$
m_j = \pm \frac{3}{2}, \pm \frac{1}{2}
$$
For the 2p_{1/2} level we have
$$
E_{2,1,\frac{1}{2}, m_j} = E_{2,1,\frac{1}{2}} + \frac{2}{3} m_j \hbar \omega_L
$$
with
$$
m_j = \pm \frac{1}{2}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should give the Zeeman-split energies for the n = 2 levels as explicit algebraic expressions in the form E_{2,0,1/2,m_j} = ..., E_{2,1,3/2,m_j} = ..., and E_{2,1,1/2,m_j} = ..., written only with E_{n l j}, m_j, ℏ, and ω_L, where ω_L = e B/(2 m_e c). You should also state the allowed m_j values for each of these levels.

subquestions.subproblem: for a hypothetical spin \mathit { \Theta } = 0 particle with electron mass.
subquestions.solution:
For a spinless particle with mass m_e there is no spin-related effect, so the Hamiltonian is
$$
\hat H = \frac{\hat p^2}{2 m_e} + V(r) + \frac{e B}{2 m_e c} \hat l_z
$$
A suitable set of eigenfunctions is
$$
\psi_{n l m}(r, \theta, \varphi) = R_{n l m}(r) Y_{l m}(\theta, \varphi)
$$
and the corresponding energies are
$$
E_{n l m} = E_{n l} + \frac{e B}{2 m_e c} m \hbar
$$
For n = 2 we have
$$
E_{2 0 0} = E_{2 0}
$$
$$
E_{2 1 0} = E_{2 1}
$$
$$
E_{2 1, \pm 1} = E_{2 1} \pm \frac{e B}{2 m_e c} \hbar
$$

Also specify the allowed m values for the l = 1 manifold (m = −1, 0, +1).

context: Consider the n = 2 levels of a hydrogen-like atom with nuclear charge Ze. Assume the spins of the orbiting particle and the nucleus are zero. Neglect all relativistic effects. Use the Coulomb potential V(r) = -Ze^2/r. Define the following symbols and operators: e > 0 is the elementary charge magnitude, m_e is the electron mass, c is the speed of light, \hbar is the reduced Planck constant, a_0 = \hbar^2/(m_e e^2) is the Bohr radius, a = a_0/Z is the effective Bohr radius, p is the canonical momentum operator, r is the radial coordinate, x and z are the Cartesian position operators for the x and z components, l_z is the z-component of the orbital angular momentum operator, and B and \varepsilon are the magnitudes of the uniform magnetic and electric fields, respectively. The unperturbed energy depends only on n and the unperturbed eigenstates are |n l m\rangle with wave functions \psi_{n l m}(r,\theta,\varphi) = R_{n l}(r) Y_{l m}(\theta,\varphi), where n = 1,2,\dots, l = 0,1,\dots,n-1, and m = -l,-l+1,\dots,l-1,l. Let E^{(1)} denote the first-order energy shift and E the total perturbed energy E = E_2 + E^{(1)} for the n = 2 manifold. Indices \mu, \nu label basis states within a degenerate subspace and \delta_{\mu\nu} is the Kronecker delta.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate to lowest order the energy splittings in the presence of a uniform magnetic field.
subquestions.solution:
Choose the z-axis along the magnetic field. The Hamiltonian is
$$H = \frac{p^2}{2 m_e} + V(r) + \frac{e B}{2 m_e c} l_z$$
$$V(r) = - \frac{Z e^2}{r}$$
Treat the Zeeman term as the perturbation
$$H' = \frac{e B}{2 m_e c} l_z$$
The unperturbed eigenstates are
$$\psi_{n l m}(r,\theta,\varphi) = R_{n l}(r) Y_{l m}(\theta,\varphi)$$
Their angular momentum expectation value is
$$\langle n l m | l_z | n l m \rangle = m \hbar$$
The first-order energy shift is
$$\Delta E_{n l m}^{(1)} = \frac{e B}{2 m_e c} m \hbar$$
For n = 2, the total energies of the four states are
$$E_{2,l=0,m=0} = E_2$$
$$E_{2,l=1,m=1} = E_2 + \frac{e B}{2 m_e c} \hbar$$
$$E_{2,l=1,m=0} = E_2$$
$$E_{2,l=1,m=-1} = E_2 - \frac{e B}{2 m_e c} \hbar$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include: (i) the general first-order Zeeman shift in the form \Delta E_{nlm}^{(1)} = ... written using the symbols e, B, m_e, c, m, \hbar; and (ii) the total energies for the n = 2 states with (l, m) = (0, 0), (1, 0), and (1, \pm 1) in the form E_{2,l=...,m=...} = E_2 + ... written using only E_2, e, B, m_e, c, \hbar.

subquestions.subproblem: Do the same for the case of a uniform electric field.
subquestions.solution:
For n = 2, the unperturbed energy is
$$E_2 = - \frac{Z^2 e^2}{2 a_0} \frac{1}{2^2}$$
The corresponding degenerate states are the four states \psi_{200}, \psi_{210}, \psi_{211}, and \psi_{21,-1}. Take a uniform electric field along the z-axis. The perturbation is
$$H' = e \varepsilon z$$
Introduce the parameters
$$E_0 = e \varepsilon a_0$$
$$V' = \frac{z}{a_0}$$
$$H' = E_0 V'$$
Use the spherical harmonic identity
$$\cos \theta\, Y_{l m} = \sqrt{\frac{(l+1)^2 - m^2}{(2 l + 1)(2 l + 3)}} Y_{l+1, m} + \sqrt{\frac{l^2 - m^2}{(2 l + 1)(2 l - 1)}} Y_{l-1, m}$$
The selection rules are
$$\Delta l = \pm 1$$
$$\Delta m = 0$$
Within the n = 2 manifold, the only nonvanishing matrix elements are
$$(H')_{200,210} = \int \psi_{200}^* H' \psi_{210} d^3 x$$
$$(H')_{210,200} = \int \psi_{210}^* H' \psi_{200} d^3 x$$
Define the parameter
$$E' = (H')_{200,210}$$
$$E' = (H')_{210,200}$$
The secular equation for the first-order shifts is
$$\det\,| H_{\mu\nu} - E^{(1)} \delta_{\mu\nu} | = 0$$
The roots are
$$E^{(1)} = E'$$
$$E^{(1)} = - E'$$
$$E^{(1)} = 0$$
$$E^{(1)} = 0$$
Therefore the perturbed energies in the n = 2 manifold are
$$E_{2,+} = E_2 + E'$$
$$E_{2,0} = E_2$$
$$E_{2,-} = E_2 - E'$$
The level at E_{2,0} is twofold degenerate.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should list the four first-order Stark shifts for the n = 2 manifold and the corresponding total energies, in the forms E^{(1)} = ... (four values) and E_{2,+} = E_2 + ..., E_{2,0} = E_2 + ..., E_{2,-} = E_2 + ..., with all expressions written only in terms of E_2 and a single parameter E'. Do not introduce any other variables.

subquestions.subproblem: Do the same for both fields present simultaneously and at right angles to each other. (Any integral over radial wave functions need not be evaluated; it can be replaced by a parameter for the rest of the calculation. The same may be done for any integral over angular wave function, once you have ascertained that it does not vanish.)
subquestions.solution:
Take the magnetic field along the z-axis and the electric field along the x-axis. The perturbation Hamiltonian is
$$H' = \frac{e B}{2 m_e c} l_z + e \varepsilon x$$
Define
$$\beta = \frac{e B \hbar}{2 m_e c}$$
$$\gamma = \frac{3 e \varepsilon a}{\sqrt{2}}$$
$$a = \frac{a_0}{Z}$$
Equivalently,
$$H' = \beta \frac{l_z}{\hbar} + \frac{\sqrt{2} \gamma}{3 a} x$$
The nonvanishing matrix elements of x are
$$(x)_{l, m-1}^{l-1, m} = \frac{3}{4} n \sqrt{\frac{(n^2 - l^2)(l - m + 1)(l - m)}{(2 l + 1)(2 l - 1)}} a$$
$$(x)_{l-1, m}^{l, m-1} = \frac{3}{4} n \sqrt{\frac{(n^2 - l^2)(l - m + 1)(l - m)}{(2 l + 1)(2 l - 1)}} a$$
$$(x)_{l - 1, m - 1}^{l, m} = - \frac{3}{4} n \sqrt{\frac{(n^2 - l^2)(l + m - 1)(l + m)}{(2 l + 1)(2 l - 1)}} a$$
$$(x)_{l, m}^{l - 1, m - 1} = - \frac{3}{4} n \sqrt{\frac{(n^2 - l^2)(l + m - 1)(l + m)}{(2 l + 1)(2 l - 1)}} a$$
For n = 2, the relevant matrix elements are
$$x_{0,0}^{1,1} = - \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} a$$
$$x_{1,1}^{0,0} = - \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} a$$
$$x_{1,-1}^{0,0} = \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} a$$
$$x_{0,0}^{1,-1} = \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} a$$
In the subspace spanned by |2,1,1\rangle, |2,1,-1\rangle, and |2,0,0\rangle, the secular equation is
$$\det\,\begin{vmatrix} \beta - E^{(1)} & 0 & - \gamma \\ 0 & - \beta - E^{(1)} & \gamma \\ - \gamma & \gamma & - E^{(1)} \end{vmatrix} = 0$$
The roots are
$$E_1^{(1)} = 0$$
$$E_2^{(1)} = \sqrt{\beta^2 + 2 \gamma^2}$$
$$E_3^{(1)} = - \sqrt{\beta^2 + 2 \gamma^2}$$
Hence the energies in the n = 2 manifold are
$$E_{2,0} = E_2$$
$$E_{2,+} = E_2 + \sqrt{\beta^2 + 2 \gamma^2}$$
$$E_{2,-} = E_2 - \sqrt{\beta^2 + 2 \gamma^2}$$
The state |2,1,0\rangle is uncoupled and also has zero first-order shift.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should give the three distinct total energies in the n = 2 manifold in the presence of mutually perpendicular uniform fields, in the form E_{2,0} = E_2 + ..., E_{2,+} = E_2 + ..., and E_{2,-} = E_2 + ..., written exclusively with the symbols E_2, \beta, \gamma.

context: Two distinguishable particles, each of mass m, are confined in one dimension to an impenetrable box with hard walls at x=0 and x=L. Let x_1 and x_2 denote the particle coordinates. The reduced Planck constant is denoted by \hbar. The single-particle normalized eigenfunctions and energies in this box are defined by ψ_n(x)=\sqrt{2/L} \sin(n \pi x/L) and E_n^{1p}=\hbar^2 \pi^2 n^2/(2 m L^2). Define the two-particle product basis states by ψ_{n k}(x_1,x_2)=ψ_n(x_1) ψ_k(x_2), with unperturbed two-particle energies E_{n k}^{(0)}=E_n^{1p}+E_k^{1p}. Consider the three lowest-energy two-particle states with (n,k) in {(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)}. An interaction potential V_{12}(x_1,x_2)=\lambda \delta(x_1-x_2) is added, where \lambda is a real coupling constant and \delta is the Dirac delta distribution. Compute, to first order in \lambda, the energy corrections for these three states, and give their wave functions to zeroth order in \lambda. For clarity, write total energies as E^{tot}=E^{(0)}+E^{(1)}. In the degenerate subspace spanned by ψ_{12} and ψ_{21}, use the perturbation matrix elements W_{ab}=\int_0^L\int_0^L ψ_a(x_1,x_2) V_{12}(x_1,x_2) ψ_b(x_1,x_2) dx_1 dx_2 to obtain the first-order corrections and zeroth-order eigenfunctions.
solution:
Unperturbed single-particle eigenfunctions and energies:

$$
ψ_n(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{L}} \sin\frac{n \pi x}{L}
$$

$$
E_n^{1p}=\frac{\hbar^2 \pi^2 n^2}{2 m L^2}
$$

Two-particle product states and unperturbed two-particle energies:

$$
ψ_{n k}(x_1,x_2)=ψ_n(x_1) ψ_k(x_2)
$$

$$
E_{n k}^{(0)}=E_n^{1p}+E_k^{1p}
$$

Three lowest unperturbed two-particle states:

$$
E_{11}^{(0)}=\frac{\hbar^2 \pi^2}{m L^2}
$$

$$
ψ_{11}(x_1,x_2)=\frac{2}{L} \sin\frac{\pi x_1}{L} \sin\frac{\pi x_2}{L}
$$

$$
E_{12}^{(0)}=\frac{5 \hbar^2 \pi^2}{2 m L^2}
$$

$$
ψ_{12}(x_1,x_2)=\frac{2}{L} \sin\frac{\pi x_1}{L} \sin\frac{2 \pi x_2}{L}
$$

$$
E_{21}^{(0)}=\frac{5 \hbar^2 \pi^2}{2 m L^2}
$$

$$
ψ_{21}(x_1,x_2)=\frac{2}{L} \sin\frac{2 \pi x_1}{L} \sin\frac{\pi x_2}{L}
$$

Interaction potential:

$$
V_{12}(x_1,x_2)=\lambda \delta(x_1-x_2)
$$

Non-degenerate ground state first-order correction:

$$
E_{11}^{(1)}=\int_0^L\int_0^L ψ_{11}(x_1,x_2) V_{12}(x_1,x_2) ψ_{11}(x_1,x_2) dx_1 dx_2
$$

$$
E_{11}^{(1)}=\lambda \int_0^L [ψ_{11}(x,x)]^2 dx
$$

$$
E_{11}^{(1)}=\frac{4 \lambda}{L^2} \int_0^L \sin^4 \frac{\pi x}{L} dx
$$

$$
\int_0^L \sin^4 \frac{\pi x}{L} dx=\frac{3 L}{8}
$$

$$
E_{11}^{(1)}=\frac{3 \lambda}{2 L}
$$

Zeroth-order ground-state wave function in the presence of the interaction:

$$
\phi_{11}^{(0)}(x_1,x_2)=ψ_{11}(x_1,x_2)
$$

Degenerate subspace perturbation matrix elements with a,b in {(1,2),(2,1)}:

$$
W_{12,12}=\int_0^L\int_0^L ψ_{12}(x_1,x_2) V_{12}(x_1,x_2) ψ_{12}(x_1,x_2) dx_1 dx_2
$$

$$
W_{12,12}=\lambda \int_0^L [ψ_{12}(x,x)]^2 dx
$$

$$
W_{12,12}=\frac{\lambda}{L}
$$

$$
W_{21,21}=\int_0^L\int_0^L ψ_{21}(x_1,x_2) V_{12}(x_1,x_2) ψ_{21}(x_1,x_2) dx_1 dx_2
$$

$$
W_{21,21}=\frac{\lambda}{L}
$$

$$
W_{12,21}=\int_0^L\int_0^L ψ_{12}(x_1,x_2) V_{12}(x_1,x_2) ψ_{21}(x_1,x_2) dx_1 dx_2
$$

$$
W_{12,21}=\lambda \int_0^L ψ_{12}(x,x) ψ_{21}(x,x) dx
$$

$$
W_{12,21}=\frac{\lambda}{L}
$$

$$
W_{21,12}=\frac{\lambda}{L}
$$

First-order energy corrections obtained by diagonalizing the 2\times 2 matrix with entries W_{ab}:

$$
E_{+}^{(1)}=\frac{2 \lambda}{L}
$$

$$
E_{-}^{(1)}=0
$$

Corresponding zeroth-order eigenfunctions in the degenerate subspace:

$$
\phi_{+}^{(0)}(x_1,x_2)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \big( ψ_{12}(x_1,x_2)+ψ_{21}(x_1,x_2) \big)
$$

$$
\phi_{-}^{(0)}(x_1,x_2)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \big( ψ_{12}(x_1,x_2)-ψ_{21}(x_1,x_2) \big)
$$

Total energies to first order in \lambda:

$$
E_{11}^{tot}=E_{11}^{(0)}+E_{11}^{(1)}
$$

$$
E_{+}^{tot}=E_{12}^{(0)}+E_{+}^{(1)}
$$

$$
E_{-}^{tot}=E_{12}^{(0)}+E_{-}^{(1)}
$$
final_answer_instructions:
Your final answer should present explicit algebraic expressions for: (i) the first-order energy correction and zeroth-order wave function of the non-degenerate (n,k)=(1,1) state, and its total energy; and (ii) the first-order energy corrections, zeroth-order eigenfunctions, and total energies for the two states obtained from the degenerate subspace spanned by ψ_{12} and ψ_{21}. Write your results in the following labeled forms, using only the variables λ, L, ℏ, m, x_1, and x_2 (and standard constants such as π):

- E_{11}^{tot} = ...

- E_{+}^{tot} = ... and E_{-}^{tot} = ...
For the wave functions, express them explicitly as functions of x_1 and x_2 with sine functions and L (do not introduce any additional symbols). context: Consider a three-level system described by the Hermitian Hamiltonian. $$H=H_0+\lambda H_1$$ The parameter lambda is real. The orthonormal eigenstates of H0 are |1>, |2>, and |3>, with unperturbed energies given by $$H_0|1\rangle=0$$ $$H_0|2\rangle=\Delta|2\rangle$$ $$H_0|3\rangle=\Delta|3\rangle$$ Here Delta is a real energy parameter. subquestions.subproblem: When the spectrum of H is computed using perturbation theory, it is found that the eigenstates of H to lowest order in lambda are |1>, |+> and |->, where |+> = (|2> + |3>)/sqrt{2} and |-> = (|2> - |3>)/sqrt{2}. The corresponding eigenvalues are $$E_1=-\frac{\lambda^2}{\Delta}+O(\lambda^3)$$ $$E_+=A+\lambda+\frac{\lambda^2}{\Delta}+O(\lambda^3)$$ $$E_-=A-\lambda+O(\lambda^3)$$ Determine as many of the matrix elements of H1 from part (a) as you can.
subquestions.solution: $$|+\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\big(|2\rangle+|3\rangle\big)$$ $$|-\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\big(|2\rangle-|3\rangle\big)$$ $$\langle+|H_1|+\rangle=1$$ $$\langle-|H_1|-\rangle=-1$$ $$\langle+|H_1|+\rangle=\frac{1}{2}(b+c+f+f^*)$$ $$\langle-|H_1|-\rangle=\frac{1}{2}(b+c-f-f^*)$$ $$b=0$$ $$c=0$$ $$f=f^*=1$$ $$E_m=E_m^{(0)}+\lambda H'_{mm}+\lambda^2\sum_{n=\,n\ne m}\frac{|H'_{mn}|^2}{E_m^{(0)}-E_n^{(0)}}+O(\lambda^3)$$ $$E_1=0+\lambda a+\frac{\lambda^2|d+e|^2}{2(0-\Delta)}+\frac{\lambda^2|d-e|^2}{2(0-\Delta)}+O(\lambda^3)$$ $$E_1=\lambda a-\frac{\lambda^2}{2\Delta}(|d+e|^2+|d-e|^2)+O(\lambda^3)$$ $$E_+=\Delta+\lambda+\frac{\lambda^2}{\Delta}\cdot\frac{1}{2}|d+e|^2+O(\lambda^3)$$ $$E_-=\Delta-\lambda+\frac{\lambda^2}{\Delta}\cdot\frac{1}{2}|d-e|^2+O(\lambda^3)$$ $$a=0$$ $$|d+e|^2+|d-e|^2=2$$ $$|d+e|^2=2$$ $$|d-e|^2=0$$ $$d+e=\sqrt{2}e^{i\delta}$$ $$d-e=0$$ $$d=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}e^{i\delta}$$ $$e=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}e^{i\delta}$$ $$H_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}e^{i\delta}&\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}e^{i\delta}\\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}e^{-i\delta}&0&1\\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}e^{-i\delta}&1&0\end{pmatrix}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as the explicit matrix H1 = [[...]] in the ordered basis { |1>, |2>, |3> }, and your response should be written using only the parameter δ (delta) in addition to numerical constants; do not introduce any other variables.

subquestions.subproblem: Write down the most general 3 x 3 matrix representation of H1 in the { |1>, |2>, |3> } basis.
subquestions.solution: $$H_1=\begin{pmatrix}a&d&e\\ d^*&b&f\\ e^*&f^*&c\end{pmatrix}$$ Here a, b, c are real numbers

context: Consider a two-dimensional oscillator with Cartesian coordinates x and y and conjugate momenta p_x and p_y. The Hamiltonian is $$H=\frac{1}{2}(p_x^2+p_y^2)+\frac{1}{2}(x^2+y^2)$$ We adopt units such that $$\hbar=1$$ $$m=1$$ $$\omega=1$$ Stationary states are labeled by nonnegative integers n_1 and n_2. The total quantum number is $$N=n_1+n_2$$ Hermite polynomials are denoted by H_i, where the argument u is a real variable. The normalization constant N_{n_1 n_2} is defined by $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\lvert\psi_{n_1 n_2}(x,y)\rvert^2 dx dy=1$$ In first-order perturbation theory, E^{(1)} denotes the first-order energy correction. For the N=1 degenerate subspace, we define the basis states by $$\psi_1=\psi_{10}$$ $$\psi_2=\psi_{01}$$ and the matrix elements by $$V_{ij}=\langle\psi_i\lvert V\rvert\psi_j\rangle$$ The small, real, dimensionless perturbation parameter satisfies $$\varepsilon\ll 1$$

subquestions.subproblem: What are the wave functions and energies of the 3 lowest states?
subquestions.solution: The general eigenfunctions are $$\psi_{n_1 n_2}(x,y)=N_{n_1 n_2} e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2} H_{n_1}(x) H_{n_2}(y)$$ The energies are $$E_{n_1 n_2}=n_1+n_2+1$$ Using the relation $$E_{n_1 n_2}=N+1$$ and the lowest Hermite polynomials $$H_0(u)=1$$ $$H_1(u)=2u$$ the three lowest states are $$\psi_{00}(x,y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2}$$ $$E_{00}=1$$ $$\psi_{10}(x,y)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{\pi}} x e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2}$$ $$E_{10}=2$$ $$\psi_{01}(x,y)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{\pi}} y e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2}$$ $$E_{01}=2$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should list the explicit normalized wave functions and energies of the three lowest states in the format: psi_00(x,y)=..., E_00=..., psi_10(x,y)=..., E_10=..., psi_01(x,y)=..., E_01=.... Use only x and y as variables in the wave functions.

subquestions.subproblem: Next consider a perturbation to the Hamiltonian $$V=\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon x y (x^2+y^2)$$ with small parameter $$\varepsilon\ll 1$$ Compute to first order in perturbation theory the effect of V on the energies of the states calculated in part (a)
subquestions.solution: For the ground state, the first-order correction is $$V_{00}=\langle\psi_{00}\lvert V\rvert\psi_{00}\rangle$$ $$V_{00}=0$$ For the N=1 degenerate subspace with basis states defined by $$\psi_1=\psi_{10}$$ $$\psi_2=\psi_{01}$$ the diagonal matrix elements are $$V_{11}=0$$ $$V_{22}=0$$ and the off-diagonal elements satisfy $$V_{12}=V_{21}$$ Using the normalized states, $$V_{12}=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{2}{\pi} x y e^{-(x^2+y^2)} x y (x^2+y^2) dx dy$$ $$V_{12}=\frac{\varepsilon}{\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-(x^2+y^2)} (x^2+y^2) x^2 y^2 dx dy$$ $$V_{12}=\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}$$ The secular equation for the first-order shifts is $$(V_{11}-E^{(1)})(V_{22}-E^{(1)} )-V_{12}V_{21}=0$$ Therefore, the corrected energies of the N=1 doublet are $$E'_{N=1,\pm}=2\pm\frac{3}{4}\varepsilon$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should give the first-order corrected energies in the format: E'_00=..., E'_{N=1,+}=..., E'_{N=1,-}=.... Use only the perturbation parameter ε (and constants) in your expressions where applicable.

grading_standard.formula: $$V_{12}=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{2}{\pi} x y e^{-(x^2+y^2)} x y (x^2+y^2) dx dy$$

context:
A nonrelativistic particle of mass m moves in three-dimensional Cartesian coordinates x, y, z under the potential
$$V=\frac{1}{2}k(x^2+y^2+z^2+\lambda x y)$$
Here k>0 is a spring constant, λ is a small dimensionless parameter, and ħ is the reduced Planck constant. Define the oscillator frequency
$$\omega=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$$
The unperturbed energies are
$$E_{n_x n_y n_z}^{(0)}=(n_x+n_y+n_z+\frac{3}{2})\hbar\omega$$
The corresponding normalized product eigenstates are denoted by kets |n_x,n_y,n_z>, and the one-dimensional ground-state wavefunctions are ψ_0(q) for q in {x,y,z}. The perturbation to be used is
$$H'=\frac{k\lambda}{2}x y$$
Use E^{(1)} and E^{(2)} for the first- and second-order energy corrections, respectively, and E_0^{(0)} for the unperturbed ground-state energy. Denote the corrected ground-state energy through second order by E_{0,corr}. Use δ_{ij} for the Kronecker delta. In part (b), let a and a^+ be the ladder operators of the x-oscillator, with analogous operators for y and z, satisfying
$$[a,a^+]=1$$
and
$$x=\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2 m \omega}}(a+a^+)$$
In the first-excited manifold, use the ordered basis |1,0,0>, |0,1,0>, |0,0,1>. Denote the 3×3 identity matrix by I_3. Report the determinant equation for the first-order correction E_1^{(1)} and the split energy levels E_{1,+}, E_{1,0}, and E_{1,-}.

subquestions.subproblem: Treat λ as a small parameter and calculate the ground-state energy through second order in perturbation theory.
subquestions.solution:
The ground-state wavefunction factorizes as
$$\psi_{000}(x,y,z)=\psi_0(x)\psi_0(y)\psi_0(z)$$
The unperturbed ground-state energy is
$$E_0^{(0)}=\frac{3}{2}\hbar\omega$$
The perturbation is
$$H'=\frac{k\lambda}{2}x y$$
The first-order correction is
$$E^{(1)}=\langle 0,0,0|H'|0,0,0\rangle$$
By parity, this vanishes
$$E^{(1)}=0$$
The relevant matrix elements are
$$\langle 0,0,0|H'|n_x,n_y,n_z\rangle=\frac{\lambda\hbar\omega}{4}\delta_{1 n_x}\delta_{1 n_y}\delta_{0 n_z}$$
The second-order correction is
$$E^{(2)}=\sum_{n_x,n_y,n_z}\frac{|\langle 0,0,0|H'|n_x,n_y,n_z\rangle|^2}{E_0^{(0)}-E_{n_x n_y n_z}^{(0)}}$$
Evaluating the sum gives
$$E^{(2)}=-\frac{\lambda^2}{32}\hbar\omega$$
Therefore, the ground-state energy through second order is
$$E_{0,corr}=\hbar\omega\left(\frac{3}{2}-\frac{\lambda^2}{32}\right)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of E_{0,corr} = ... , and your response should be written with \hbar, \omega, \lambda.

subquestions.subproblem:
Treat λ as a small parameter and calculate the first-excited energy levels to first order in perturbation theory. Use the standard one-dimensional harmonic-oscillator formulas:
$$\omega=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$$
$$E_n=\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)\hbar\omega$$
$$x=\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2 m \omega}}(a+a^+)$$
$$a\psi_n=\sqrt{n}\psi_{n-1}$$
$$[a,a^+]=1$$
$$a^+\psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}\psi_{n+1}$$
subquestions.solution:
The unperturbed first-excited energy is
$$E_1^{(0)}=\frac{5}{2}\hbar\omega$$
Define the basis states in this subspace as
$$B_1=|1,0,0\rangle$$
$$B_2=|0,1,0\rangle$$
$$B_3=|0,0,1\rangle$$
With H' as defined, the perturbation matrix in the basis {B_1,B_2,B_3} is
$$H'_{deg}=\frac{\lambda\hbar\omega}{4}\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\1&0&0\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$$
The secular equation is
$$\det(H'_{deg}-E_1^{(1)} I_3)=0$$
The first-order energy corrections are
$$E_{1,+}^{(1)}=\frac{\lambda\hbar\omega}{4}$$
$$E_{1,0}^{(1)}=0$$
$$E_{1,-}^{(1)}=-\frac{\lambda\hbar\omega}{4}$$
Thus, the split first-excited energy levels are
$$E_{1,+}=\left(\frac{5}{2}+\frac{\lambda}{4}\right)\hbar\omega$$
$$E_{1,0}=\frac{5}{2}\hbar\omega$$
$$E_{1,-}=\left(\frac{5}{2}-\frac{\lambda}{4}\right)\hbar\omega$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Provide two parts: (1) The secular determinant equation in the form \det(H'_{deg} - E_1^{(1)} I_3) = 0, with H'_{deg} expressed using \lambda, \hbar, \omega and I_3; and (2) the split first-excited energy levels in the form E_{1,+} = ..., E_{1,0} = ..., E_{1,-} = ..., with each expression written using \hbar, \omega, \lambda.

context: Consider two one-electron atoms. Each electron of mass m is bound to a very massive nucleus by a harmonic potential. The potential for electron i at position vector r_i (measured from its own nucleus) is given by $$V(r_i)=\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 r_i^2$$ Assume the two nuclei are fixed along the x-axis and separated by a distance d satisfying $$d \gg \sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{m \omega}}$$ Let x_i be the x-coordinate of electron i, and let e be the elementary charge magnitude. The electrons interact via a weak coupling modeled by the perturbation $$V_{12}=\beta \frac{e^2}{d^3} x_1 x_2$$ where \beta is a dimensionless parameter. Let E be the total energy and \Psi the total wave function of the two-electron system. Denote by \psi_n(x) the nth one-dimensional harmonic-oscillator eigenfunction in coordinate x, and similarly for y and z. The unperturbed two-particle ground state is denoted by \Psi_0^{(0)}(r_1,r_2). The excited product state with n=1 in the x-motion of each particle and n=0 in all other coordinates is denoted by $$\Psi_1^{(0)}=\psi_1(x_1)\psi_0(y_1)\psi_0(z_1)\psi_1(x_2)\psi_0(y_2)\psi_0(z_2)$$

subquestions.subproblem: Consider the ground state of the entire system when β = 0. Give its energy and wave function in terms of r_1 and r_2.
subquestions.solution: The time-independent Schrödinger equation for the full system is $$\Big[-\frac{\hbar^2}{2 m}(\nabla_1^2+\nabla_2^2)+\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2(r_1^2+r_2^2)+\beta \frac{e^2}{d^3} x_1 x_2\Big] \Psi=E \Psi$$ For \beta=0 the system reduces to two independent three-dimensional harmonic oscillators. The ground-state energy is $$E_0^{(0)}=\frac{3}{2} \hbar \omega+\frac{3}{2} \hbar \omega$$ $$E_0^{(0)}=3 \hbar \omega$$ The ground-state wave function is $$\Psi_0^{(0)}(r_1,r_2)=\psi_0(x_1)\psi_0(y_1)\psi_0(z_1)\psi_0(x_2)\psi_0(y_2)\psi_0(z_2)$$ $$\Psi_0^{(0)}(r_1,r_2)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} e^{-\frac{m \omega}{2 \hbar}(r_1^2+r_2^2)}$$ with $$r_1^2=x_1^2+y_1^2+z_1^2$$ $$r_2^2=x_2^2+y_2^2+z_2^2$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include two expressions: E_0^{(0)} = ... and Ψ_0^{(0)}(r_1, r_2) = ... . Your response should be written only with the variables m, ω, ħ, r_1, and r_2, and it should present the wave function explicitly in terms of r_1 and r_2.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the lowest nonzero correction to the energy, ΔE, and to the wave function due to V_12.
subquestions.solution: Treat the perturbation as $$H'=\frac{\beta e^2}{d^3} x_1 x_2$$ The first-order correction to the ground-state energy is $$\Delta E_0^{(1)}=\langle 00|H'|00\rangle$$ $$\Delta E_0^{(1)}=0$$ since each factor satisfies \langle 0|x|0\rangle=0. Here |n_1 n_2\rangle denotes the product state with x-quantum numbers n_1 for particle 1 and n_2 for particle 2, with all y and z modes in their ground states. For the second-order correction, the relevant matrix element is $$\langle 00|H'|n_1 n_2\rangle=\frac{\beta e^2}{d^3}\langle 0|x_1|n_1\rangle\langle 0|x_2|n_2\rangle$$ $$\langle 00|H'|n_1 n_2\rangle=\frac{\beta e^2}{d^3}\frac{\hbar}{2 m \omega} \delta_{n_1,1} \delta_{n_2,1}$$ Hence $$\Delta E_0^{(2)}=\sum_{n_1,n_2\neq 0} \frac{|\langle 00|H'|n_1 n_2\rangle|^2}{E_0-E_{n_1 n_2}}$$ $$\Delta E_0^{(2)}=\frac{|\langle 00|H'|11\rangle|^2}{E_0-E_{11}}$$ $$\Delta E_0^{(2)}=-\frac{1}{2 \hbar \omega}\Big(\frac{\beta e^2}{d^3}\frac{\hbar}{2 m \omega}\Big)^2$$ using $$E_{n_1 n_2}=(n_1+\frac{3}{2})\hbar \omega+(n_2+\frac{3}{2})\hbar \omega$$ Therefore the ground-state energy to lowest nonzero order is $$E_0=3 \hbar \omega-\frac{1}{8}\Big(\frac{e^2}{d^3}\Big)^2 \frac{\hbar}{m^2 \omega^3} \beta^2$$ The corrected ground-state wave function to lowest order is $$\Psi_0=\Psi_0^{(0)}+\frac{\langle 00|H'|11\rangle}{E_0-E_{11}}\Psi_1^{(0)}$$ $$\Psi_0=\Psi_0^{(0)}-\lambda \Psi_1^{(0)}$$ with $$\lambda=\frac{\beta e^2}{4 d^3} \frac{1}{m \omega^2}$$ and $$\Psi_1^{(0)}=\psi_1(x_1)\psi_0(y_1)\psi_0(z_1)\psi_1(x_2)\psi_0(y_2)\psi_0(z_2)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include two expressions: ΔE = ... (the lowest nonzero correction to the ground-state energy) and Ψ_0 = ... (the ground-state wave function to lowest order in β). Your response should be written only with the symbols β, e, d, m, ω, ħ, Ψ_0^{(0)}, and Ψ_1^{(0)}. If you introduce a coefficient multiplying Ψ_1^{(0)}, you must give that coefficient explicitly in terms of β, e, d, m, and ω.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the r.m.s. separation along the x direction of the two electrons to lowest order in β. The one-dimensional harmonic-oscillator wave functions and matrix elements you may use are $$\psi_0(x)=\pi^{-1/4} e^{-\frac{m \omega x^2}{2 \hbar}}$$ $$\psi_1(x)=\pi^{-1/4}\Big(\frac{2 m \omega}{\hbar}\Big)^{1/2} x e^{-\frac{m \omega x^2}{2 \hbar}}$$ $$\langle n-1|x|n\rangle=\Big(\frac{n \hbar}{2 m \omega}\Big)^{1/2}$$ $$\langle n+1|x|n\rangle=\Big(\frac{(n+1) \hbar}{2 m \omega}\Big)^{1/2}$$
subquestions.solution: Define the relative electronic displacement along x as $$S_{12}=x_2-x_1$$ By symmetry $$\langle S_{12}\rangle=0$$ Hence $$\langle S_{12}^2\rangle=\langle x_1^2+x_2^2-2 x_1 x_2\rangle$$ $$\langle S_{12}^2\rangle=2 \langle x_1^2\rangle-2 \langle x_1 x_2\rangle$$ Using $$\Psi_0=\Psi_0^{(0)}-\lambda \Psi_1^{(0)}$$ we find $$\langle x_1 x_2\rangle=\langle \Psi_0^{(0)}-\lambda \Psi_1^{(0)}|x_1 x_2|\Psi_0^{(0)}-\lambda \Psi_1^{(0)}\rangle$$ To first order in \lambda, the cross term gives the only contribution, and adding its complex conjugate yields $$\langle x_1 x_2\rangle=-2 \lambda\big(\langle 0|x|1\rangle\big)^2$$ $$\langle x_1 x_2\rangle=-\lambda \frac{\hbar}{m \omega}$$ with $$\lambda=\frac{\beta e^2}{4 d^3} \frac{1}{m \omega^2}$$ For the single-particle variance, to order O(\lambda^2) we have $$\langle x_1^2\rangle=\langle \Psi_0^{(0)}-\lambda \Psi_1^{(0)}|x_1^2|\Psi_0^{(0)}-\lambda \Psi_1^{(0)}\rangle$$ $$\langle x_1^2\rangle=\langle 0|x^2|0\rangle+O(\lambda^2)$$ Using the virial theorem for the harmonic oscillator $$\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 \langle 0|x^2|0\rangle=\frac{1}{4} \hbar \omega$$ which gives $$2 \langle x_1^2\rangle=\frac{\hbar}{m \omega}+O(\lambda^2)$$ Therefore $$\langle S_{12}^2\rangle=\frac{\hbar}{m \omega}+\frac{2 \hbar}{m \omega} \lambda+O(\lambda^2)$$ The root-mean-square x-separation of the electrons, including the fixed nuclear separation d, is $$\sqrt{\langle(d+S_{12})^2\rangle}=\sqrt{d^2+2 d \langle S_{12}\rangle+\langle S_{12}^2\rangle}$$ $$\sqrt{\langle(d+S_{12})^2\rangle}\approx \sqrt{d^2+\frac{\hbar}{m \omega}(1+2 \lambda)}$$ $$\sqrt{\langle(d+S_{12})^2\rangle}=d \sqrt{1+\frac{\hbar}{m \omega d^2}\Big(1+\frac{\beta e^2}{2 m \omega^2 d^3}\Big)}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should give the x-direction root-mean-square separation in the form √⟨(d + x_2 − x_1)^2⟩ = ... , evaluated to lowest order in β. Your response should be written only with the variables d, m, ω, ħ, β, and e, without introducing additional symbols.

context:
The first excited state of a three-dimensional isotropic harmonic oscillator, with natural angular frequency \(\omega_0\) and particle mass \(m\), is three-fold degenerate. Using first-order degenerate perturbation theory, calculate the energy splitting to first order caused by the small perturbation \(H' = b x y\), where \(b\) is a constant. Give the first-order wave functions of the three split levels in terms of the wave functions of the unperturbed three-dimensional harmonic oscillator.

Definitions and notation to be used:
- The unperturbed 3D oscillator eigenkets are
$$
|n_x n_y n_z\rangle = |n_x\rangle |n_y\rangle |n_z\rangle
$$
- The total quantum number is \(n = n_x + n_y + n_z\) with unperturbed energy
$$
E_n^{(0)} = \left(n + \frac{3}{2}\right) \hbar \omega_0
$$
- The first excited manifold \(n=1\) consists of
$$
|100\rangle,\ |010\rangle,\ |001\rangle
$$
- For a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator of mass \(m\) and frequency \(\omega_0\), the matrix element is
$$
\langle n|x|n+1\rangle = \sqrt{\frac{(n+1)\hbar}{2 m \omega_0}}
$$
Provide the three first-order energy shifts and the corresponding normalized first-order wave functions.
solution:
Write the unperturbed product basis as
$$
|n_x n_y n_z\rangle = |n_x\rangle |n_y\rangle |n_z\rangle
$$
Introduce the degenerate first excited states
$$
|\psi_1\rangle = |100\rangle
$$
$$
|\psi_2\rangle = |010\rangle
$$
$$
|\psi_3\rangle = |001\rangle
$$
Compute the matrix elements of the perturbation in this basis
$$
H'_{ij} = b \langle \psi_i| x y |\psi_j\rangle
$$
For the diagonal elements
$$
\langle 100| x y |100\rangle = \langle 1|x|1\rangle \langle 0|y|0\rangle
$$
$$
\langle 1|x|1\rangle = 0
$$
$$
H'_{11} = 0
$$
By the same parity argument
$$
H'_{22} = 0
$$
$$
H'_{33} = 0
$$
For the off-diagonal element between \(|100\rangle\) and \(|010\rangle\)
$$
H'_{12} = b \langle 100| x y |010\rangle
$$
$$
\langle 100| x y |010\rangle = \langle 1|x|0\rangle \langle 0|y|1\rangle
$$
Using the 1D matrix element
$$
\langle 0|x|1\rangle = \sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2 m \omega_0}}
$$
Hermiticity gives
$$
\langle 1|x|0\rangle = \sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2 m \omega_0}}
$$
Similarly
$$
\langle 0|y|1\rangle = \sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2 m \omega_0}}
$$
Therefore
$$
H'_{12} = \frac{\hbar b}{2 m \omega_0}
$$
By Hermiticity
$$
H'_{21} = \frac{\hbar b}{2 m \omega_0}
$$
For the couplings to \(|001\rangle\)
$$
H'_{13} = b \langle 100| x y |001\rangle
$$
$$
\langle 100| x y |001\rangle = \langle 1|x|0\rangle \langle 0|y|0\rangle
$$
$$
\langle 0|y|0\rangle = 0
$$
$$
H'_{13} = 0
$$
By the same reasoning
$$
H'_{31} = 0
$$
$$
H'_{23} = 0
$$
$$
H'_{32} = 0
$$
Thus the perturbation matrix in the ordered basis \(|100\rangle, |010\rangle, |001\rangle\) is
$$
H' = \frac{\hbar b}{2 m \omega_0} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
$$
The secular equation is
$$
\det\big(H' - E^{(1)} I\big) = 0
$$
Its roots are
$$
E^{(1)} = 0
$$
$$
E^{(1)} = \frac{\hbar b}{2 m \omega_0}
$$
$$
E^{(1)} = -\frac{\hbar b}{2 m \omega_0}
$$
The unperturbed energy of the \(n=1\) manifold is
$$
E^{(0)} = \frac{5}{2} \hbar \omega_0
$$
The total first-order energies are
$$
E_0 = E^{(0)} + 0
$$
$$
E_+ = E^{(0)} + \frac{\hbar b}{2 m \omega_0}
$$
$$
E_- = E^{(0)} - \frac{\hbar b}{2 m \omega_0}
$$
The corresponding normalized first-order eigenkets are
$$
|\psi_0^{(1)}\rangle = |001\rangle
$$
$$
|\psi_+^{(1)}\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \big(|100\rangle + |010\rangle\big)
$$
$$
|\psi_-^{(1)}\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \big(|100\rangle - |010\rangle\big)
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include the three first-order energy shifts and the corresponding normalized first-order eigenkets. Present them in the format: E_+^{(1)} = ..., E_-^{(1)} = ..., E_0^{(1)} = ..., each expressed only in terms of b, \hbar, m, and \omega_0; and |\psi_+^{(1)}\rangle = ..., |\psi_-^{(1)}\rangle = ..., |\psi_0^{(1)}\rangle = ..., each written explicitly as a normalized linear combination of the unperturbed basis states |100\rangle, |010\rangle, and |001\rangle, using only these kets and numerical coefficients.

context: A quantum mechanical system is described by the total Hamiltonian H = H_0 + H_Δ, where the perturbation is H_Δ = i λ [A, H_0]. Here A and B are Hermitian operators and λ is a real number. Define the Hermitian operator C = i [B, A]. The commutator is [X, Y] = XY − YX. The unperturbed ground state of H_0 is assumed nondegenerate; expectation values in this state are denoted ⟨O⟩_0 for any operator O, and expectation values in the perturbed ground state are denoted ⟨O⟩. In part b we use the three-dimensional isotropic harmonic oscillator with canonical operators x_i and p_i (i = 1, 2, 3), mass m, angular frequency ω, and reduced Planck constant ħ, satisfying [x_i, p_j] = i ħ δ_{ij}.

subquestions.subproblem: You are given the expectation values of the operators A, B, and C in the unperturbed nondegenerate ground state, denoted ⟨A⟩_0, ⟨B⟩_0, and ⟨C⟩_0, where C = i [B, A]. With the perturbation switched on, evaluate the expectation value of B in the perturbed ground state to first order in λ. Then, apply your result to the three-dimensional isotropic harmonic oscillator by choosing A = p_3/(m ω^2 ħ) and B ∈ {x_1, x_2, x_3}.
subquestions.solution:
To first order in λ, the expectation value of B in the perturbed ground state is
$$
\langle B \rangle \approx \langle B \rangle_0 + \lambda \langle C \rangle_0
$$
For the three-dimensional isotropic harmonic oscillator, choose
$$
A = \frac{p_3}{m \omega^2 \hbar}
$$
For B = x_1 we have
$$
C_1 = i [x_1, A]
$$
$$
C_1 = \frac{i}{m \omega^2 \hbar} [x_1, p_3]
$$
$$
[x_1, p_3] = 0
$$
$$
C_1 = 0
$$
$$
\langle x_1 \rangle \approx \langle x_1 \rangle_0 + \lambda \langle C_1 \rangle_0
$$
$$
\langle x_1 \rangle_0 = 0
$$
$$
\langle C_1 \rangle_0 = 0
$$
$$
\langle x_1 \rangle = 0
$$
For B = x_2 we have
$$
C_2 = i [x_2, A]
$$
$$
C_2 = \frac{i}{m \omega^2 \hbar} [x_2, p_3]
$$
$$
[x_2, p_3] = 0
$$
$$
C_2 = 0
$$
$$
\langle x_2 \rangle \approx \langle x_2 \rangle_0 + \lambda \langle C_2 \rangle_0
$$
$$
\langle x_2 \rangle_0 = 0
$$
$$
\langle x_2 \rangle = 0
$$
For B = x_3 we have
$$
C_3 = i [x_3, A]
$$
$$
C_3 = i \left[ x_3, \frac{p_3}{m \omega^2 \hbar} \right]
$$
$$
[x_3, p_3] = i \hbar
$$
$$
C_3 = -\frac{1}{m \omega^2}
$$
$$
\langle C_3 \rangle_0 = -\frac{1}{m \omega^2}
$$
$$
\langle x_3 \rangle \approx \langle x_3 \rangle_0 + \lambda \langle C_3 \rangle_0
$$
$$
\langle x_3 \rangle_0 = 0
$$
$$
\langle x_3 \rangle = -\frac{\lambda}{m \omega^2}
$$
An exact solution for the oscillator with perturbation H_Δ = λ x_3 is obtained by completing the square
$$
H = \sum_{i=1}^3 \left( \frac{p_i^2}{2 m} + \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 x_i^2 \right) + \lambda x_3
$$
$$
H = H_{01}(x_1) + H_{02}(x_2) + \frac{p_3^2}{2 m} + \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 \left( x_3 + \frac{\lambda}{m \omega^2} \right)^2 - \frac{\lambda^2}{2 m \omega^2}
$$
$$
H_{0i}(x_i) = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2 m} \frac{d^2}{d x_i^2} + \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 x_i^2
$$
The exact ground-state wavefunction is
$$
\psi_0(x_1, x_2, x_3) = \left( \frac{m \omega}{\pi \hbar} \right)^{3/4} \exp \left( - \frac{m \omega}{2 \hbar} x_1^2 \right) \exp \left( - \frac{m \omega}{2 \hbar} x_2^2 \right) \exp \left( - \frac{m \omega}{2 \hbar} \left( x_3 + \frac{\lambda}{m \omega^2} \right)^2 \right)
$$
From this exact state we obtain
$$
\langle x_1 \rangle = 0
$$
$$
\langle x_2 \rangle = 0
$$
$$
\langle x_3 \rangle = -\frac{\lambda}{m \omega^2}
$$

context:
A spin-1/2 particle of mass m moves in the three-dimensional isotropic harmonic oscillator potential V = 1/2 m omega^2 r^2 and is subject to a perturbation lambda sigma dot r. Spin-orbit forces are ignored. The position operator is r, the momentum operator is P, the oscillator angular frequency is omega, the reduced Planck constant is hbar, sigma is the vector of Pauli matrices, and lambda is a real coupling constant. The total and unperturbed Hamiltonians are
$$
H = H_0 + H'
$$
$$
H_0 = \frac{P^2}{2 m} + \frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 r^2
$$
$$
H' = \lambda \sigma \cdot r
$$
Let the unperturbed oscillator-spin product eigenstates be denoted by | n_x n_y n_z s \rangle, where n_x, n_y, n_z in {0,1,2,...} are the one-dimensional quantum numbers and s in {\uparrow, \downarrow} labels the spin eigenstate along an arbitrary quantization axis. The unperturbed energies are
$$
E_{n_x n_y n_z}^{(0)} = \left(n_x + n_y + n_z + \frac{3}{2}\right) \hbar \omega
$$
Define the ground-manifold states by | g, s \rangle = | 0 0 0 s \rangle. For each i in {x,y,z}, define the first-excited spatial states | e_i, s \rangle by setting n_i = 1 and the other two quantum numbers equal to 0, with the same spin label s. Let x_i denote the Cartesian coordinate operators, with x_x = x, x_y = y, x_z = z.
solution:
The unperturbed ground state is two-fold degenerate due to spin. First-order degenerate perturbation theory requires diagonalizing H' within the subspace spanned by | g, \uparrow \rangle and | g, \downarrow \rangle. The matrix elements vanish because the ground-state expectation value of each Cartesian coordinate is zero, hence
$$
\langle g, s | H' | g, s' \rangle = 0
$$
Therefore
$$
\Delta E_{0,s}^{(1)} = 0
$$
For the second-order correction, sum over intermediate unperturbed eigenstates | \mu \rangle and spin labels s'. The general expression is
$$
\Delta E_{0,s}^{(2)} = \sum_{\mu,s'} \frac{| \langle g, s | H' | \mu, s' \rangle |^2}{E_0^{(0)} - E_{\mu}^{(0)}}
$$
Only the three first-excited spatial states | e_i, s' \rangle contribute through the dipole matrix elements of r. The relevant one-dimensional harmonic-oscillator matrix element is
$$
\langle n_i | x_i | n_i + 1 \rangle = \sqrt{\frac{(n_i+1) \hbar}{2 m \omega}}
$$
Thus for the ground-to-first transition in three dimensions
$$
| \langle g | x_i | e_i \rangle |^2 = \frac{\hbar}{2 m \omega}
$$
The unperturbed ground and first-excited energies are
$$
E_0^{(0)} = \frac{3}{2} \hbar \omega
$$
$$
E_{e_i}^{(0)} = \frac{5}{2} \hbar \omega
$$
so the energy denominator is
$$
E_0^{(0)} - E_{e_i}^{(0)} = - \hbar \omega
$$
Using H' = lambda sigma dot r and the factorization of spatial and spin parts, one has
$$
| \langle g, s | H' | e_i, s' \rangle |^2 = \lambda^2 | \langle g | x_i | e_i \rangle |^2 | \langle s | \sigma_i | s' \rangle |^2
$$
The spin sum for each Cartesian component satisfies
$$
\sum_{s'} | \langle s | \sigma_i | s' \rangle |^2 = 1
$$
Collecting the three Cartesian contributions gives
$$
\Delta E_{0,s}^{(2)} = - \frac{3 \lambda^2}{2 m \omega^2}
$$
Therefore the ground-state energy remains two-fold degenerate and equals
$$
E_{0,s} = \frac{3}{2} \hbar \omega - \frac{3 \lambda^2}{2 m \omega^2}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form E_{0,s} = ... , and it must be an explicit algebraic expression written only in terms of \hbar, \omega, \lambda, and m (no other symbols, constants, or numerical approximations).

grading_standard.formula: $$| \langle g, s | H' | e_i, s' \rangle |^2 = \lambda^2 | \langle g | x_i | e_i \rangle |^2 | \langle s | \sigma_i | s' \rangle |^2$$

context: Consider a spinless particle of mass m and charge e confined in a spherical cavity of radius R. The potential energy is V(r)=0 for 0≤r≤R and V(r)=+∞ for r>R. Work in Gaussian units. The speed of light is c and the reduced Planck constant is ℏ. Use Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) and spherical coordinates (r,θ,φ) with z=r cosθ. The canonical momentum operator is p=−iℏ∇. The orbital angular momentum operator is L=r×p with z-component L_z. The unperturbed Hamiltonian is H_0=p^2/(2m)+V(r). The spherical Bessel function of the first kind is j_ℓ, and the spherical harmonics are Y_{ℓm}. The unperturbed ground state has ℓ=0 with radial factor j_0(kr), where k is fixed by the boundary condition j_0(kR)=0. A uniform magnetic field of magnitude B=|B| along +z is represented by the symmetric gauge A_x=−(B/2)y, A_y=(B/2)x, A_z=0. A uniform electric field of magnitude E=|E| along +z has perturbing potential U_E=−eEz. The symbol E_0 denotes the ground-state energy in the context specified within each subproblem.

subquestions.subproblem: Suppose that a weak uniform magnetic field of strength | \mathbf { B } | is switched on. Calculate the shift in the ground state energy.
subquestions.solution:
Choose the magnetic field along +z with the symmetric gauge
$$A_x=-\frac{B}{2}y$$
$$A_y=\frac{B}{2}x$$
$$A_z=0$$
The Hamiltonian with minimal coupling is
$$H=\frac{1}{2 m}\left(p+\frac{e}{c}A\right)^2+V(r)$$
Expanding to second order in B gives
$$H=\frac{p^2}{2 m}-\frac{e B}{2 m c}L_z+\frac{e^2 B^2}{8 m c^2}(x^2+y^2)+V(r)$$
Treat the magnetic terms as a perturbation for a weak field
$$W=-\frac{e B}{2 m c}L_z+\frac{e^2 B^2}{8 m c^2}(x^2+y^2)$$
For the spherically symmetric ground state with ℓ=0 we have
$$\langle L_z\rangle_0=0$$
A convenient form of the ground-state wavefunction is
$$\psi_0(r,θ,φ)=\frac{\sin(kr)}{\sqrt{2\pi R}\,r}$$
with
$$k=\frac{\pi}{R}$$
The first-order energy shift is
$$\Delta E_B=\langle 0|W|0\rangle$$
Thus
$$\Delta E_B=\frac{e^2 B^2}{8 m c^2}\langle x^2+y^2\rangle_0$$
Using the identities
$$x^2+y^2=r^2\sin^2\theta$$
$$\langle r^2\rangle_0=R^2\left(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2\pi^2}\right)$$
we obtain
$$\langle x^2+y^2\rangle_0=\frac{2}{3}\langle r^2\rangle_0$$
Hence
$$\Delta E_B=\frac{e^2 B^2 R^2}{12 m c^2}\left(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2\pi^2}\right)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of ΔE_B = ..., and your response should be written using only e, B, m, c, and R (universal constants such as π may appear).

subquestions.subproblem: Suppose that, instead, a weak uniform electric field of strength IEl is switched on. Will the ground state energy increase or decrease? Write down, but do not attempt to evaluate, a formula for the shift in the ground state energy.
subquestions.solution:
Take the electric field along +z. The perturbing potential energy is
$$U_E=-e E r\cos\theta$$
The first-order shift of the ground-state energy is
$$\Delta E_E=\langle \psi(r,\theta,\phi)|-e E r\cos\theta|\psi(r,\theta,\phi)\rangle$$
As stated, this shift is negative, so the ground state energy decreases
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include both of the following: (1) a single sentence stating exactly one of 'The ground state energy increases.' or 'The ground state energy decreases.'; and (2) an unevaluated first-order perturbation-theory expression for the shift written in the form ΔE_E = ⟨0| − e E z |0⟩. Your expression should use only e, E, and z (with |0⟩ denoting the unperturbed ground state).

subquestions.subproblem: If, instead, a very strong magnetic field of strength $| \mathbf { B } |$ is turned on, approximately what would be the ground state energy?
subquestions.solution:
For a very strong magnetic field, the Hamiltonian is effectively
$$H=\frac{p^2}{2 m}+\frac{e^2 B^2}{8 m c^2}(x^2+y^2)$$
Identify the two-dimensional harmonic oscillator frequency from
$$\frac{1}{2}m\omega^2=\frac{e^2 B^2}{8 m c^2}$$
which gives
$$\omega=\frac{e B}{2 m c}$$
The approximate ground-state energy is
$$E_0=\hbar\omega$$
Hence
$$E_0=\frac{e B}{2 m c}\hbar$$

context: A particle of mass m and electric charge Q moves in a three-dimensional isotropic harmonic-oscillator potential V = 1/2 k r^2 with r^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2. The oscillator angular frequency is defined by ω_0 = sqrt(k/m). The reduced Planck constant is ħ and c is the speed of light. Let Ĥ denote the Hamiltonian operator. Let the canonical momentum operators be ĥp_x, ĥp_y, ĥp_z, collected as the vector ĥp. In part (b), a uniform external electric field of magnitude E may be applied along the z axis; the symbol E denotes that field magnitude, and the constant term −Q^2 E^2/(2 k) in energies vanishes when E = 0. In part (c), a uniform magnetic field of magnitude B is applied along the z axis. Define ω = |Q| B/(2 m c) and ω′ = sqrt(ω^2 + ω_0^2). The z-component of orbital angular momentum operator ĥL_z has eigenvalues m_φ ħ with azimuthal quantum number m_φ ∈ {0, ±1, ±2, …}. In part (c), use quantum numbers (n_ρ, n_z, m_φ) with n_ρ, n_z ∈ {0, 1, 2, …}. When the coupling term is written as ∓ ω ĥL_z, take the minus sign for Q > 0 and the plus sign for Q < 0.

subquestions.subproblem: If a uniform electric field is applied, what are the new energy levels and their degeneracies?
subquestions.solution:
Take the direction of the uniform electric field as the z axis. The Hamiltonian is
$$\hat H = \frac{\hat{p}_x^2 + \hat{p}_y^2 + \hat{p}_z^2}{2 m} + \frac{1}{2} k r^2 - Q E z$$
$$\hat H = \frac{\hat p_x^2}{2 m} + \frac{1}{2} k x^2 + \frac{\hat p_y^2}{2 m} + \frac{1}{2} k y^2 + \frac{\hat p_z^2}{2 m} + \frac{1}{2} k \left(z - \frac{Q E}{k}\right)^2 - \frac{Q^2 E^2}{2 k}$$
The spectrum is that of the three-dimensional isotropic oscillator, uniformly shifted by the Stark constant term, with the same degeneracies:
$$E_N^{(E)} = \left(N + \frac{3}{2}\right) \hbar \omega_0 - \frac{Q^2 E^2}{2 k}$$
$$f(N) = \frac{1}{2} (N + 1) (N + 2)$$

subquestions.subproblem: If, instead, a uniform magnetic field is applied, what are the energies of the four lowest states?
subquestions.solution:
In cylindrical coordinates, choose the vector potential components
$$A_{\varphi} = \frac{1}{2} B \rho$$
$$A_{\rho} = 0$$
$$A_z = 0$$
The Hamiltonian with minimal coupling is
$$\hat H = \frac{1}{2 m} \left( \hat{\mathbf p} - \frac{Q}{c} \mathbf A \right)^2 + V$$
Expanding and using r^2 = \rho^2 + z^2 and \nabla \cdot A = 0 gives
$$\hat H = \frac{\hat{\mathbf p}^2}{2 m} - \frac{Q}{m c} \hat{\mathbf p} \cdot \mathbf A + \frac{Q^2}{2 m c^2} \mathbf A^2 + \frac{1}{2} k \rho^2 + \frac{1}{2} k z^2$$
Decompose as
$$\hat H = \hat H_t + \hat H_z \mp \omega \hat L_z$$
with
$$\hat H_t = - \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m} \nabla_t^2 + \frac{1}{2} m \omega'^2 \rho^2$$
$$\hat H_z = \frac{\hat p_z^2}{2 m} + \frac{1}{2} k z^2$$
$$\nabla_t^2 = \nabla_x^2 + \nabla_y^2$$
$$\omega = \frac{|Q| B}{2 m c}$$
$$\omega'^2 = \omega^2 + \omega_0^2$$
The energy levels are
$$E_{n_{\rho} n_z m_{\varphi}} = \left( 2 n_{\rho} + 1 + | m_{\varphi} | \right) \hbar \omega' + \left( n_z + \frac{1}{2} \right) \hbar \omega_0 \mp m_{\varphi} \hbar \omega$$
Equivalently,
$$E_{n_{\rho} n_z m_{\varphi}} = \hbar \omega' + \frac{1}{2} \hbar \omega_0 + 2 n_{\rho} \hbar \omega' + | m_{\varphi} | \hbar \omega' \mp m_{\varphi} \hbar \omega + n_z \hbar \omega_0$$
The allowed quantum numbers are
$$n_{\rho} \in \{0,1,2,\ldots\}$$
$$n_z \in \{0,1,2,\ldots\}$$
$$m_{\varphi} \in \{0,\pm 1,\pm 2,\ldots\}$$
The four lowest energy levels are
$$E_{000} = \hbar \omega' + \frac{1}{2} \hbar \omega_0$$
$$E_{001} = \hbar \omega' + \frac{1}{2} \hbar \omega_0 + \hbar ( \omega' - \omega )$$
$$E_{001} = 2 \hbar \omega' - \hbar \omega + \frac{1}{2} \hbar \omega_0$$
$$E_{010} = \hbar \omega' + \frac{1}{2} \hbar \omega_0 + \hbar \omega_0$$
$$E_{010} = \hbar \omega' + \frac{3}{2} \hbar \omega_0$$
$$E_{002} = \hbar \omega' + \frac{1}{2} \hbar \omega + 2 \hbar ( \omega' - \omega )$$
$$E_{002} = 3 \hbar \omega' - 2 \hbar \omega + \frac{1}{2} \hbar \omega_0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should list the energies of the four lowest states as four algebraic expressions labeled by their quantum numbers, each in the form E_{n_\rho n_z m_\varphi} = ..., and your response should be written using only the variables \hbar, \omega', \omega_0, \omega.

$$E_{n_{\rho} n_z m_{\varphi}} = \left( 2 n_{\rho} + 1 + | m_{\varphi} | \right) \hbar \omega' + \left( n_z + \frac{1}{2} \right) \hbar \omega_0 \mp m_{\varphi} \hbar \omega$$
$$E_{n_{\rho} n_z m_{\varphi}} = \hbar \omega' + \frac{1}{2} \hbar \omega_0 + 2 n_{\rho} \hbar \omega' + | m_{\varphi} | \hbar \omega' \mp m_{\varphi} \hbar \omega + n_z \hbar \omega_0$$

- The spin–orbit coupling strength is \xi(r)
- The reduced Planck constant is \hbar with unit \unit{J s}
- The unperturbed Hamiltonian in part (a) is \hat H_0 = \frac{\hat p^2}{2 m} + V(r) + \xi(r) \hat s \cdot \hat l, the Zeeman interaction is \hat H_1, and the total Hamiltonian is \hat H = \hat H_0 + \hat H_1
- In part (b), the spin–orbit interaction is neglected so the Hamiltonian used is \hat H = \frac{\hat p^2}{2 m} + V(r) + \hat H_1
- The fine-structure energy for fixed n, l, j is E_{n l j}; the central-field energy for fixed n, l is E_{n l}
- Stationary states are denoted \psi_{n l j m_j} in the weak-field case and \psi_{n l m_l m_s} in the strong-field case
- The Pauli matrix \sigma_z acts on spin states
- The expectation value \bar s_z denotes the expectation of \hat s_z in the indicated state
- The Landé factor is denoted g and appears via E_{n l j m_j} \approx E_{n l j} - g \mu_0 B m_j in the weak-field result
- The symbol \Delta m_s denotes the change in m_s in a transition
- Define N_{weak\_levels} as the number of Zeeman components in the weak-field limit and N_{strong\_levels} as the number of distinct energy levels in the strong-field (Paschen–Back) limit

subquestions.subproblem: Describe the splitting of atomic energy levels by a weak magnetic field. Include in your discussion a calculation of the Land6 $\mathrm { g }$ -factor (assume LS couplings).
subquestions.solution:
The Hamiltonian of the system is
$$\hat H = \hat H_0 + \hat H_1$$
The unperturbed Hamiltonian in this part is
$$\hat H_0 = \frac{\hat p^2}{2 m} + V(r) + \xi(r) \hat s \cdot \hat l$$
Treating \(-(g_s - g_l) \mu_0 B \hat s_z\) as a perturbation and operating with \(\hat H_0 - g_l \mu_0 B \hat j_z\) on the common eigenstate of \hat l^2, \hat j^2, \hat j_z gives
$$(\hat H_0 - g_l \mu_0 B \hat j_z) \psi_{n l j m_j} = (E_{n l j} - g_l \mu_0 B m_j) \psi_{n l j m_j}$$
For very weak B, the spin expectation value is
$$\bar s_z = \frac{\hbar}{2} \langle j m_j | \sigma_z | j m_j \rangle$$
For j = l + \frac{1}{2} one has
$$\bar s_z = \frac{m_j}{2 j}$$
For j = l - \frac{1}{2} one has
$$\bar s_z = - \frac{m_j}{2 (j + 1)}$$
The relations used are, for j = l \pm \frac{1}{2},
$$| j m_j \rangle = \sqrt{\frac{l \pm m_j + \frac{1}{2}}{2 l + 1}} | m_j - \frac{1}{2} , \frac{1}{2} \rangle \mp \sqrt{\frac{l \mp m_j + \frac{1}{2}}{2 l + 1}} | m_j + \frac{1}{2} , - \frac{1}{2} \rangle$$
and
$$\sigma_z | m_j \mp \frac{1}{2} , \pm \frac{1}{2} \rangle = \pm | m_j \mp \frac{1}{2} , \pm \frac{1}{2} \rangle$$
Hence the energies to first order are
$$E_{n l j m_j} \approx E_{n l j} - g_l \mu_0 B m_j$$
For j = l + \frac{1}{2} the additional contribution is
$$E_{n l j m_j} \approx E_{n l j} - g_l \mu_0 B m_j - (g_s - g_l) \mu_0 B \frac{m_j}{2 j}$$
For j = l - \frac{1}{2} the additional contribution is
$$E_{n l j m_j} \approx E_{n l j} - g_l \mu_0 B m_j - (g_s - g_l) \mu_0 B \frac{- m_j}{2 (j + 1)}$$
With the values used here
$$g_l = 1$$
$$g_s = 2$$
we can write
$$E_{n l j m_j} \approx E_{n l j} - g \mu_0 B m_j$$
with the Landé factor
$$g = - \Bigg[ 1 + \frac{j (j + 1) + s (s + 1) - l (l + 1)}{2 j (j + 1)} \Bigg]$$
Thus the number of Zeeman components is
$$N_{weak\_levels} = 2 j + 1$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Provide three algebraic results: (i) the weak-field energy splitting written in the form E_{n l j m_j} = ... using only the variables E_{n l j}, \mu_0, B, m_j, and g; (ii) the Landé factor written in the form g = ... using only the variables j, l, and s; and (iii) the number of Zeeman components written in the form N_{weak_levels} = ... using only the variable j.

subquestions.subproblem: Describe the splitting in a strong magnetic field (Paschen-Back effeet).
subquestions.solution:
In a very strong field the spin–orbit term is neglected, and the Hamiltonian used is
$$\hat H = \frac{\hat p^2}{2 m} + V(r) + \hat H_1$$
Acting on the common eigenstate of \hat H, \hat l^2, \hat l_z, \hat s^2, \hat s_z gives
$$\hat H \psi_{n l m_l m_s} = E_{n l m_l m_s} \psi_{n l m_l m_s}$$
The energies are
$$E_{n l m_l m_s} = E_{n l} - g_l \mu_0 B m_l - g_s \mu_0 B m_s$$
With the value used here
$$g_s = - 2$$
this becomes
$$E_{n l m_l m_s} = E_{n l} + \mu_0 B (m_l + 2 m_s)$$
For an electron the spin projections are
$$m_s = \frac{1}{2}$$
$$m_s = - \frac{1}{2}$$
The selection rule is
$$\Delta m_s = 0$$
The number of distinct energy levels in the Paschen–Back regime is
$$N_{strong\_levels} = 2 l + 3$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Provide: (i) the strong-field energy splitting written in the form E_{n l m_l m_s} = ... using only the variables E_{n l}, \mu_0, B, g_l, g_s, m_l, and m_s; (ii) the selection rule written in the form \Delta m_s = ...; and (iii) the number of distinct strong-field levels written in the form N_{strong_levels} = ... using only the variable l.

grading_standard.formula: $$E_{n l j m_j} \approx E_{n l j} - g_l \mu_0 B m_j$$
$$E_{n l j m_j} \approx E_{n l j} - g_l \mu_0 B m_j - (g_s - g_l) \mu_0 B \frac{m_j}{2 j}$$
$$E_{n l j m_j} \approx E_{n l j} - g_l \mu_0 B m_j - (g_s - g_l) \mu_0 B \frac{- m_j}{2 (j + 1)}$$
$$E_{n l j m_j} \approx E_{n l j} - g \mu_0 B m_j$$
$$E_{n l m_l m_s} = E_{n l} - g_l \mu_0 B m_l - g_s \mu_0 B m_s$$

context: Consider an atom with a single valence electron. The fine-structure interaction Hamiltonian is H_fs = ξ(r) S · L, where L is the electron orbital angular momentum operator with quantum number l, S is the electron spin operator with s = 1/2, and J = L + S is the total angular momentum with quantum numbers j and m_j for J_z. The principal quantum number is n. The electron linear momentum operator is p and the central potential is V(r). The external uniform magnetic field has magnitude H and is directed along the z axis. The electron mass is m_e, the elementary charge is e, the speed of light is c, and ħ is the reduced Planck constant. The Bohr magneton is μ_B = eħ/(2 m_e c). The orbital magnetic quantum number is m_l for L_z, and the spin magnetic quantum number is m_s = ± 1/2 for S_z. The spherical harmonics are Y_{l m}. The two-component spinors α and β are eigenstates of S_z with eigenvalues +ħ/2 and −ħ/2, respectively. The notation \overline{ξ(r)} denotes the radial expectation value of ξ(r) in the unperturbed state. The field-free fine-structure level energy is denoted E_{n l j}. The central-field energy without spin–orbit interaction is denoted E_{n l}. Define ΔE_fs as the fine-structure interval ΔE_fs = E_{j=l+1/2} − E_{j=l−1/2}. Define ΔE_Z as the energy splitting between adjacent Zeeman sublevels corresponding to Δm_j = 1.

subquestions.subproblem: Determine the difference in the energies of the levels characterized by J = L + 1/2 and J = L - 1/2 (fine structure interval) in terms of \xi.
subquestions.solution:
Use the operator identity in the simultaneous eigenbasis of J^2, L^2, and J_z
$$S \cdot L = \frac{1}{2} \big( J^2 - L^2 - S^2 \big)$$
Taking expectation values in an eigenstate with quantum numbers j, l, s gives
$$\langle S \cdot L \rangle = \frac{\hbar^2}{2} \big[ j(j+1) - l(l+1) - s(s+1) \big]$$
For an electron with s = \frac{1}{2}
$$\langle S \cdot L \rangle = \frac{\hbar^2}{2} \big[ j(j+1) - l(l+1) - \frac{3}{4} \big]$$
The energy of a level with total angular momentum j is
$$E_j = \overline{\xi(r)} \langle S \cdot L \rangle$$
Using j = l \pm \frac{1}{2}, the difference of the quadratic factors is
$$(l+\tfrac{1}{2})(l+\tfrac{3}{2}) - (l-\tfrac{1}{2})(l+\tfrac{1}{2}) = 2l+1$$
Therefore the fine-structure interval is
$$\Delta E_{fs} = \overline{\xi(r)} \frac{\hbar^2}{2} (2l+1)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \Delta E_{fs} = ... , and your response should be written solely with \overline{\xi(r)}, l, and \hbar.

subquestions.subproblem: This atom is placed in a weak external magnetic field of magnitude H. Use perturbation theory to determine the energy splitting between adjacent magnetic (Zeeman) sublevels of the atom.
subquestions.solution:
With a weak magnetic field H along z, the full Hamiltonian is
$$H = \frac{p^2}{2 m_e} + V(r) + \frac{eH}{2 m_e c} \big( L_z + 2 S_z \big) + \xi(r) S \cdot L$$
Choose the unperturbed Hamiltonian
$$H_0 = \frac{p^2}{2 m_e} + V(r) + \frac{eH}{2 m_e c} J_z + \xi(r) S \cdot L$$
and the perturbation
$$V' = \frac{eH}{2 m_e c} S_z$$
Let \(\psi_{n l j m_j}\) be a common eigenstate of H_0, J^2, L^2, and J_z. Then
$$H_0 \psi_{n l j m_j} = \Big( E_{n l j} + m_j \frac{eH\hbar}{2 m_e c} \Big) \psi_{n l j m_j}$$
The first-order correction is
$$\Delta E^{(1)} = \frac{eH}{2 m_e c} \langle j m_j | S_z | j m_j \rangle$$
To evaluate the matrix element, use the angular spinor expansions for j = l + \frac{1}{2}
$$\varphi_{l j m_j} = \sqrt{\frac{j + m_j}{2 j}} \alpha Y_{j - \frac{1}{2}, m_j - \frac{1}{2}} + \sqrt{\frac{j - m_j}{2 j}} \beta Y_{j - \frac{1}{2}, m_j + \frac{1}{2}}$$
For j = l - \frac{1}{2}
$$\varphi_{l j m_j} = - \sqrt{\frac{j - m_j + 1}{2 j + 2}} \alpha Y_{j + \frac{1}{2}, m_j - \frac{1}{2}} + \sqrt{\frac{j + m_j + 1}{2 j + 2}} \beta Y_{j + \frac{1}{2}, m_j + \frac{1}{2}}$$
The spinors satisfy
$$S_z \alpha = \frac{\hbar}{2} \alpha$$
$$S_z \beta = - \frac{\hbar}{2} \beta$$
Hence, for j = l + \frac{1}{2}
$$\langle j m_j | S_z | j m_j \rangle = \frac{\hbar}{2} \frac{m_j}{j}$$
For j = l - \frac{1}{2}
$$\langle j m_j | S_z | j m_j \rangle = - \frac{\hbar}{2} \frac{m_j}{j+1}$$
Therefore the total energies are
$$E_{n l j m_j} = E_{n l j} + \mu_B H \Big( 1 + \frac{1}{2j} \Big) m_j \quad \text{for} \quad j = l + \frac{1}{2}$$
$$E_{n l j m_j} = E_{n l j} + \mu_B H \Big( 1 - \frac{1}{2j+2} \Big) m_j \quad \text{for} \quad j = l - \frac{1}{2}$$
Thus, the splitting between adjacent Zeeman sublevels with Δm_j = 1 is
$$\Delta E_Z = \mu_B H \Big( 1 + \frac{1}{2j} \Big) \quad \text{for} \quad j = l + \frac{1}{2}$$
$$\Delta E_Z = \mu_B H \Big( 1 - \frac{1}{2j+2} \Big) \quad \text{for} \quad j = l - \frac{1}{2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as two expressions: \Delta E_Z = ... for j = l + \tfrac{1}{2} and \Delta E_Z = ... for j = l - \tfrac{1}{2}, expressed solely in terms of \mu_B, H, and j, and clearly indicating the applicable j-manifold (j = l \pm \tfrac{1}{2}).

subquestions.subproblem: Describe qualitatively how things change in a very strong magnetic field.
subquestions.solution:
In a very strong field the Zeeman term dominates the spin–orbit interaction
$$\xi(r) S \cdot L \ll \mu_B H$$
The Hamiltonian reduces to
$$H = \frac{p^2}{2 m_e} + V(r) + \frac{eH}{2 m_e c} \big( L_z + 2 S_z \big)$$
The good quantum numbers are n, l, m_l, and m_s, and the energies are
$$E_{n l m_l m_s} = E_{n l} + \frac{eH\hbar}{2 m_e c} ( m_l + 2 m_s )$$
Using m_s = \pm \frac{1}{2}
$$E_{n l m_l m_s} = E_{n l} + \mu_B H ( m_l \pm 1 )$$
Hence the spacing between adjacent magnetic sublevels is
$$\Delta E_Z = \mu_B H$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \Delta E_Z = ... , and your response should be written solely with \mu_B and H.

grading_standard.formula: $$H = \frac{p^2}{2 m_e} + V(r) + \frac{eH}{2 m_e c} \big( L_z + 2 S_z \big) + \xi(r) S \cdot L$$
$$H_0 = \frac{p^2}{2 m_e} + V(r) + \frac{eH}{2 m_e c} J_z + \xi(r) S \cdot L$$
$$H_0 \psi_{n l j m_j} = \Big( E_{n l j} + m_j \frac{eH\hbar}{2 m_e c} \Big) \psi_{n l j m_j}$$
$$\Delta E^{(1)} = \frac{eH}{2 m_e c} \langle j m_j | S_z | j m_j \rangle$$
$$E_{n l j m_j} = E_{n l j} + \mu_B H \Big( 1 + \frac{1}{2j} \Big) m_j \quad \text{for} \quad j = l + \frac{1}{2}$$
$$E_{n l j m_j} = E_{n l j} + \mu_B H \Big( 1 - \frac{1}{2j+2} \Big) m_j \quad \text{for} \quad j = l - \frac{1}{2}$$
$$H = \frac{p^2}{2 m_e} + V(r) + \frac{eH}{2 m_e c} \big( L_z + 2 S_z \big)$$
$$E_{n l m_l m_s} = E_{n l} + \frac{eH\hbar}{2 m_e c} ( m_l + 2 m_s )$$
$$E_{n l m_l m_s} = E_{n l} + \mu_B H ( m_l \pm 1 )$$

context: An atom is in an LS-coupled state with total electron spin quantum number S, total orbital angular momentum quantum number L, and total total angular momentum quantum number J. The z component of the total angular momentum operator is denoted by \hat J_z. The nuclear spin is ignored. A weak, uniform magnetic field of magnitude B is applied along the z direction, small enough that the fine-structure interaction remains dominant. Let e be the elementary charge, m_e the electron mass, c the speed of light, and \hbar the reduced Planck constant. Define the Bohr magneton by \mu_B = e \hbar/(2 m_e c). The magnetic quantum number M_J is defined by the eigenvalue equation \hat J_z \to J_z with J_z = \hbar M_J. Find the first-order energy shift due to the magnetic field.
solution:
The first-order Zeeman perturbation for an LS-coupled electron system in a magnetic field B along z is
$$
\hat H' = \frac{\mu_B B}{\hbar} \big( \hat L_z + 2 \hat S_z \big)
$$
Using \hat L_z = \hat J_z - \hat S_z, this can be written as
$$
\hat H' = \frac{\mu_B B}{\hbar} \big( \hat J_z + \hat S_z \big)
$$
The first-order energy shift is
$$
\Delta E = \langle \hat H' \rangle
$$
The expectation value of \hat J_z in the state with magnetic quantum number M_J is
$$
\langle \hat J_z \rangle = \hbar M_J
$$
Use the projection theorem with
$$
\hat S \cdot \hat J = \frac{1}{2} \big( \hat J^2 + \hat S^2 - \hat L^2 \big)
$$
so that
$$
\langle \hat S \cdot \hat J \rangle = \frac{\hbar^2}{2} \big( J(J+1) + S(S+1) - L(L+1) \big)
$$
and therefore
$$
\langle \hat S_z \rangle = \hbar M_J \frac{J(J+1) + S(S+1) - L(L+1)}{2 J(J+1)}
$$
Substituting these expectation values gives
$$
\Delta E = \mu_B B M_J \Bigg[ 1 + \frac{J(J+1) + S(S+1) - L(L+1)}{2 J(J+1)} \Bigg]
$$
Define the Lande factor by
$$
 g_J = 1 + \frac{J(J+1) + S(S+1) - L(L+1)}{2 J(J+1)}
$$
so that
$$
\Delta E = \mu_B B g_J M_J
$$
Using J_z = \hbar M_J, the shift expressed in terms of J_z is
$$
E_{\text{shift}} = \frac{\mu_B B}{\hbar} g_J J_z
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form E_shift = ... and must use only the symbols J, L, S, J_z, B, mu_B, and hbar (and numerical constants if needed). If you introduce any auxiliary factor such as g_J, you must explicitly define it within your final expression solely in terms of J, L, and S.

grading_standard.formula: $$\Delta E = \mu_B B M_J \Bigg[ 1 + \frac{J(J+1) + S(S+1) - L(L+1)}{2 J(J+1)} \Bigg]$$

context: A spinless, nonrelativistic particle of charge g moves in a central potential. The unperturbed Hamiltonian H0 has a fourfold-degenerate energy level consisting of the s-state |00> and the three p-states |1 m_l> with m_l=0, ±1. At time t=0, a spatially uniform electric field along z is turned on, E(t)=E0 sin(ω t). The perturbation in the dipole approximation is H' = - g E0 z sin(ω t), where z is the position operator along the z-axis. Ignore transitions to any states other than these four degenerate states and make no further approximations. The system is initially in the s-state |00> at t=0. Define Ps(t) as the occupation probability of |00>, Pp(m_l=0)(t) as the occupation probability of |10>, and Pp(m_l=±1)(t) as the occupation probabilities of |1, ±1>. Express all results in terms of the nonzero matrix element ⟨00| z |10⟩. Use ħ for the reduced Planck constant, ω for the field angular frequency, and E0 for the field amplitude.
solution:
Choose the basis {|00>, |10>, |1, -1>, |1, +1>} and denote the state vector components by ψ(t)=(x1, x2, x3, x4)^T with x1↔|00>, x2↔|10>, x3↔|1, -1>, x4↔|1, +1>. The full Hamiltonian is
$$
H = H_0 + H'
$$
$$
H' = - g E_0 z \sin \omega t
$$
Within this subspace the only nonzero z-matrix element that couples |00> is
$$
\langle 10| z |00 \rangle \ne 0
$$
All couplings to |1,\pm 1> vanish
$$
\langle 1,\pm 1| z |00 \rangle = 0
$$
The initial condition is
$$
\psi(0) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}
$$
Define the real coupling constant
$$
\lambda = g E_0 \langle 00| z |10 \rangle
$$
The time-dependent Schrödinger equation for the coupled subspace spanned by x1 and x2 is
$$
i \hbar \frac{d}{dt} \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{pmatrix} = - \lambda \sin \omega t \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{pmatrix}
$$
The remaining components obey
$$
i \hbar \frac{d x_3}{d t} = 0
$$
$$
i \hbar \frac{d x_4}{d t} = 0
$$
With x3(0)=0 we have
$$
x_3(t) = 0
$$
With x4(0)=0 we have
$$
x_4(t) = 0
$$
Diagonalize the 2x2 coupling by defining
$$
a = \frac{x_1 + x_2}{\sqrt{2}}
$$
$$
b = \frac{x_1 - x_2}{\sqrt{2}}
$$
These obey
$$
i \hbar \frac{d a}{d t} = - \lambda \sin \omega t \; a
$$
$$
i \hbar \frac{d b}{d t} = \lambda \sin \omega t \; b
$$
The initial conditions are
$$
a(0) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
$$
$$
b(0) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
$$
The solutions are
$$
a(t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \exp\left( i \frac{\lambda}{\hbar \omega} \left( 1 - \cos \omega t \right) \right)
$$
$$
b(t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \exp\left( - i \frac{\lambda}{\hbar \omega} \left( 1 - \cos \omega t \right) \right)
$$
Transforming back gives
$$
x_1(t) = \frac{a(t) + b(t)}{\sqrt{2}}
$$
$$
x_2(t) = \frac{a(t) - b(t)}{\sqrt{2}}
$$
Introduce
$$
\theta(t) = \frac{\lambda}{\hbar \omega} \left( 1 - \cos \omega t \right)
$$
Then
$$
x_1(t) = \cos \theta(t)
$$
$$
x_2(t) = i \sin \theta(t)
$$
The occupation probability of |00> is
$$
P_s(t) = \cos^2 \theta(t)
$$
The occupation probability of |10> is
$$
P_{p(m_l=0)}(t) = \sin^2 \theta(t)
$$
The occupation probability of |1,-1> is
$$
P_{p(m_l=-1)}(t) = 0
$$
The occupation probability of |1,+1> is
$$
P_{p(m_l=+1)}(t) = 0
$$
Here \langle 00| z |10 \rangle is real and can be evaluated from the central-field eigenfunctions R_{nl}(r) and Y_{lm}(\theta,\varphi)
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of Ps(t) = ..., Pp(m_l=0)(t) = ..., Pp(m_l=+1)(t) = ..., and Pp(m_l=-1)(t) = ..., and your expressions should be written using only g, E0, ⟨00| z |10⟩, ħ, ω, and t. Do not introduce any additional symbols or parameters.

context: An ion of a certain atom has orbital angular momentum quantum number L=1 and spin S=0 in free space. The ion is implanted at x=y=z=0 inside a crystalline solid and experiences the local electrostatic environment of four point charges as shown in Fig. 5.19. The perturbation Hamiltonian is H'=H_1+H_2, where H_1 represents the lowest-order crystal-field anisotropy proportional to L_x^2-L_y^2 with real coupling constant alpha, and H_2 is the Zeeman interaction with an external magnetic field B directed along the z axis, with coupling coefficient beta such that the Zeeman term is (beta B/ hbar)L_z. The orbital raising and lowering operators are defined by L_+=L_x+iL_y and L_-=L_x-iL_y. Throughout, |L,M_L> denotes an eigenstate of L^2 and L_z with L=1 and M_L in {-1,0,1}. Planck's constant divided by 2pi is denoted by hbar.

subquestions.subproblem: Express the perturbation Hamiltonian H'=H_1+H_2 in terms of the orbital angular momentum raising and lowering operators L_+ and L_-.
subquestions.solution:
From the definitions of the ladder operators
$$L_+=L_x+iL_y$$
$$L_-=L_x-iL_y$$
we have the commutator
$$[L_+,L_-]=2\hbar L_z$$
and the identity
$$L_x^2-L_y^2=\frac{1}{2}(L_+^2+L_-^2)$$
Thus the perturbation Hamiltonian in Cartesian components is
$$H'=\frac{\alpha}{\hbar^2}(L_x^2-L_y^2)+\frac{\beta B}{\hbar}L_z$$
and in terms of L_+ and L_- it is
$$H'=\frac{\alpha}{2\hbar^2}(L_+^2+L_-^2)+\frac{\beta B}{2\hbar^2}(L_+L_- - L_-L_+)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of H' = ... expressed solely in terms of the operators L_+ and L_- and the constants alpha, beta, B, and hbar.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the matrix of the perturbation Hamiltonian in the basis set using the three states |1,0>, |1,1> and |1,-1>.
subquestions.solution:
Using the action of the ladder operators
$$L_\pm|L,M_L\rangle=\hbar\sqrt{L(L+1)-M_L(M_L\pm1)}|L,M_L\pm1\rangle$$
we obtain for L=1 the nonvanishing actions
$$L_-^2|1,1\rangle=2\hbar^2|1,-1\rangle$$
$$L_+^2|1,-1\rangle=2\hbar^2|1,1\rangle$$
$$L_+L_-|1,1\rangle=2\hbar^2|1,1\rangle$$
$$L_+L_-|1,0\rangle=2\hbar^2|1,0\rangle$$
$$L_-L_+|1,0\rangle=2\hbar^2|1,0\rangle$$
$$L_-L_+|1,-1\rangle=2\hbar^2|1,-1\rangle$$
In the ordered basis {|1,1>, |1,0>, |1,-1>} the matrix representation of H' is
$$\begin{pmatrix} \beta B & 0 & \alpha \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \alpha & 0 & -\beta B \end{pmatrix}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be the 3x3 matrix representation of H' in the ordered basis {|1,1>, |1,0>, |1,-1>}, with all entries expressed using only alpha, beta, and B.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the energy levels of the ion as a function of B. Make a careful sketch of your result.
subquestions.solution:
Let the state vector be expanded as a|1,1>+b|1,0>+c|1,-1> with components (a,b,c)^T. The eigenvalue equation is
$$\begin{pmatrix} \beta B - E & 0 & \alpha \\ 0 & -E & 0 \\ \alpha & 0 & -\beta B - E \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$$
The secular equation is
$$\det\begin{pmatrix} \beta B - E & 0 & \alpha \\ 0 & -E & 0 \\ \alpha & 0 & -\beta B - E \end{pmatrix}=0$$
The energy corrections are
$$E_1=-\sqrt{(\beta B)^2+\alpha^2}$$
$$E_2=0$$
$$E_3=\sqrt{(\beta B)^2+\alpha^2}$$
The perturbation energy levels as functions of B are shown in Fig. 5.20
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should provide explicit algebraic expressions for the three energy levels as functions of B, written only in terms of alpha, beta, and B (for example, list E1(B), E2(B), and E3(B)).

subquestions.subproblem: When B=0, what are the eigenfunctions describing the ion?
subquestions.solution:
For B=0 the energy levels are
$$E_1=-\alpha$$
$$E_2=0$$
$$E_3=\alpha$$
From the eigenvalue problem, the component relations for the corresponding eigenvectors (in the ordered basis {|1,1>, |1,0>, |1,-1>}) are
$$a=-c$$
$$b=0$$
$$a\neq 0$$
$$a=0$$
$$c=0$$
$$b\neq 0$$
$$a=c$$
$$b=0$$
$$a\neq 0$$
A convenient normalized choice is
$$\begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{pmatrix}_{(1)}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$$
$$\begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{pmatrix}_{(2)}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$$
$$\begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{pmatrix}_{(3)}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$$
Therefore, the normalized eigenkets are
$$|E_1=-\alpha\rangle=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|1,1\rangle+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|1,-1\rangle$$
$$|E_2=0\rangle=|1,0\rangle$$
$$|E_3=\alpha\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|1,1\rangle+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|1,-1\rangle$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should list the three normalized eigenfunctions at B=0 as linear combinations of the basis kets |1,1>, |1,0>, and |1,-1> with numerical coefficients (for example, provide |E1>, |E2>, and |E3>).
